ग्रामीण खाप पंचायतें लड़कियों और महिलाओं को मोबाइल फोन का उपयोग करने से रोकती हैं, यह कहकर कि यह 'संस्कृति' के खिलाफ है। क्या तकनीक तक पहुंच लैंगिक समानता की लड़ाई नहीं है?
मनरेगा (MGNREGA) श्रमिकों की उपस्थिति अब एक ऐप के माध्यम से दर्ज की जाती है, लेकिन खराब इंटरनेट कनेक्टिविटी के कारण उनकी मजदूरी काट ली जाती है। क्या तकनीक ने श्रमिक अधिकारों को कमजोर किया है?

शिकारी ऋण ऐप्स (Predatory Loan Apps) ग्रामीण लोगों की संपर्क सूची (Contacts) चुरा लेते हैं और ऋण न चुकाने पर उनके रिश्तेदारों को परेशान करते हैं। डिजिटल साक्षरता की कमी का लाभ उठाने वालों को कैसे रोका जाए?
फूड डिलीवरी ऐप्स '10 मिनट में डिलीवरी' का वादा करते हैं, जिससे डिलीवरी पार्टनर अपनी जान जोखिम में डालकर गाड़ी चलाते हैं। क्या उपभोक्ता की सुविधा श्रमिक की सुरक्षा से अधिक महत्वपूर्ण है?
गिग इकॉनमी (Gig Economy) वर्कर्स को 'पार्टनर' कहा जाता है ताकि उन्हें कर्मचारी लाभ (PF, बीमा) न देना पड़े, जबकि एल्गोरिदम उन पर कड़ा नियंत्रण रखता है। क्या यह श्रम कानूनों का डिजिटल उल्लंघन है?

एक एड-टेक स्टार्टअप अपने सेल्स कर्मचारियों पर गरीब माता-पिता को महंगे कोर्स बेचने का दबाव डालता है, यह जानते हुए कि वे कर्ज में डूब जाएंगे। क्या विकास (Growth) के लिए नैतिकता को ताक पर रखा जा सकता है?
बेंगलुरु के स्टार्टअप्स कर्मचारियों के लैपटॉप पर 'की-लॉगर' सॉफ्टवेयर स्थापित करते हैं ताकि घर से काम करते समय उनकी उत्पादकता की निगरानी की जा सके। विश्वास और निगरानी के बीच की रेखा क्या है?
UPI भुगतान ऐप्स उपयोगकर्ताओं के खर्च करने के पैटर्न का डेटा एकत्र करते हैं और उसे विज्ञापनदाताओं को बेचते हैं। भारत में डेटा सुरक्षा कानून की कमी का फायदा उठाना कितना नैतिक है?
क्विक-कॉमर्स 'डार्क स्टोर्स' आवासीय क्षेत्रों में रात भर शोर और ट्रैफिक पैदा करते हैं, जिससे स्थानीय निवासियों को परेशानी होती है। क्या स्टार्टअप्स को नागरिक नियमों से छूट मिलनी चाहिए?
एक एआई स्टार्टअप ने हजारों कर्मचारियों को एक ज़ूम कॉल पर नौकरी से निकाल दिया। क्या डिजिटल माध्यम ने मानवीय संवेदना और कॉर्पोरेट जिम्मेदारी को खत्म कर दिया है?
कैब एग्रीगेटर ऐप्स पीक आवर्स के दौरान कीमतों में वृद्धि (Surge Pricing) करते हैं, लेकिन ड्राइवरों की कमाई नहीं बढ़ाते। क्या एल्गोरिदम केवल कंपनी के मुनाफे के लिए धांधली कर रहा है?

You are a developer for a government digital ID app intended to streamline welfare. The security protocol requires a fixed residential address for 2FA verification code mailing. This requirement immediately excludes the 5,000 homeless individuals the app is meant to help. Do you bypass the security standard, risking fraud, or launch a compliant system that blocks the primary users?

A homeless client has lost their physical ID documents for the third time due to camp sweeps. You run a non-profit that offers a cloud-based 'Digital Locker' for personal docs. However, accessing the locker requires biometric authentication (face/fingerprint). The client refuses, citing fear that biometric data will be subpoenaed by police to track them. Do you refuse them service or build a less secure password-only tier?

You are designing a 'Smart City' access pass that consolidates library, transit, and shelter access. The system creates a permanent digital footprint of a user's movement. To make the system work for houseless people without smartphones, you must issue RFID wristbands. Critics argue this is 'digital branding' of the poor. How do you proceed?

A job application platform uses AI to parse resumes. It automatically down-ranks or rejects applications listing 'General Delivery' or known shelter addresses as the applicant's location. You are the product manager. Fixing this requires a costly retraining of the core algorithm and manual whitelisting. Is the cost justifiable for a user base with 'low conversion potential'?

Banks are closing physical branches, moving to online-only KYC (Know Your Customer). The online process requires uploading a utility bill to prove residency. You are a regulator. Do you mandate banks accept 'shelter residency letters'—which banks argue are easily forged—or allow the financial exclusion of the unhoused to continue?

A telemedicine app for street medicine requires a permanent callback number to schedule follow-ups. Most patients rely on burner phones with changing numbers or public Wi-Fi. Do you create a 'store-and-forward' message system that holds sensitive medical info until the patient checks in, risking privacy breaches, or stick to the phone requirement that causes 60% of patients to miss care?

You are building a voting registration interface. The law requires a 'place of residence.' You can allow users to drop a pin on a map (e.g., a park bench or underpass), but this data becomes public record. Publishing the exact sleeping locations of vulnerable people puts them at risk of harassment. Do you obfuscate the location, potentially violating election transparency laws?

A blockchain project offers 'Self-Sovereign Identity' (SSI) to the homeless, giving them ownership of their data. However, if they lose their private key (stored on a device that is often stolen or broken), their identity is irretrievable forever. Do you implement a centralized 'custodian' backdoor, defeating the purpose of SSI, or accept that some users will become permanently digitally non-existent?

A city shelter requires all residents to sign in via a facial recognition kiosk to prevent double-dipping on meals and beds. The system is donated by a tech giant, but the Terms of Service allow the company to use the facial data to train their surveillance algorithms. As the shelter director, do you accept the free, efficient tech or return to paper logs and reduced capacity?

To secure funding, a shelter must participate in the HMIS (Homeless Management Information System). A new local ordinance requires HMIS data to be shared with the police department to 'track fugitives.' You know this will cause your undocumented and wary guests to flee back to the streets. Do you comply to keep the lights on, or refuse and close the shelter?

A 'Smart Shelter' uses IoT sensors to monitor bed occupancy, temperature, and noise levels. The data reveals that a specific resident frequently talks to themselves at night (mental health struggle), disrupting the 'sleep efficiency score' of the room. The algorithm suggests evicting them to improve the metric for the other 20 people. Do you follow the data?

You are installing a Wi-Fi network for a shelter. The donor stipulates that 'inappropriate content' must be blocked. The filter aggressively blocks sites related to harm reduction (needle exchanges), sexual health, and LGBTQ+ support, labeling them 'adult content.' Do you accept the filtered internet which is better than nothing, or fight the donor and risk losing the network?

A shelter uses an algorithmic lottery system to allocate beds. The algorithm prioritizes 'vulnerability,' but defines it based on interaction with police and hospitals. This penalizes the 'quiet homeless' who avoid systems. Do you tweak the algorithm to randomize selection, potentially leaving a dying person on the street, or stick to the data-driven triage?

RFID tags are sewn into shelter blankets and coats to prevent theft. A local store installs a scanner that detects these tags to identify and ban shelter residents from entering. You are the shelter tech lead. Do you remove the anti-theft tags, losing inventory you can't replace, or keep them and allow your residents to be profiled?

A family shelter offers free tablets for children to do homework. The tablets come with pre-installed spyware that allows staff to monitor all communications 'for child safety.' A teenager uses the tablet to confidentially report abuse by a shelter staff member. The accused staff member sees the log. How do you design a reporting system that bypasses your own surveillance?

To manage overcrowding, a city proposes a 'Virtual Shelter' app where users check in via GPS to reserve a designated safe camping spot on public land. If the phone battery dies or GPS drifts, the spot is revoked and police are dispatched to clear the area. Is this a helpful organization tool or a digital curfew?

You manage a coffee shop chain going 100% cashless for efficiency and safety. This effectively bans local homeless residents who only use cash from buying food or using the bathroom. Do you create a 'charity card' workaround that identifies them as charity cases, or maintain a single cash register that slows down the whole operation?

A street performer app allows passersby to tip buskers via QR code. The platform takes a 15% cut and reports income to the tax authority. For a homeless busker receiving disability benefits, this traceable income could disqualify them from their lifeline aid. Do you build the app knowing it might destroy their safety net?

Public transit moves to a contactless-only system (phone or credit card). There is no cash option on the bus. A program offers free transit cards to the homeless, but the cards are tracked, and travel patterns are analyzed to 'optimize social services.' Is freedom of movement worth the loss of privacy?

A 'Digital Alms' kiosk is proposed for the city center. People donate to the machine, and the funds are distributed to registered homeless individuals via a restricted debit card that prohibits purchase of alcohol or tobacco. Is this an effective way to increase donations, or a paternalistic control mechanism that violates autonomy?

Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDC) are introduced. The government issues 'expiry-dated' stimulus tokens to the homeless to encourage immediate spending in the local economy. This prevents them from saving for a deposit on an apartment. Do you design the token with an expiry date to ensure food security now, or without it to allow future mobility?

A homeless individual finds a prepaid debit card. It has no name, but using it requires a PIN. They manage to guess it. Is using these digital funds theft, or scavenging? As a programmer for the card company, do you implement geolocation locking that freezes the card if used in a 'high-crime' (homeless) area?

Cryptocurrency is pitched as a way for the unbanked to hold assets. A homeless encampment pools their money into a shared wallet. The volatility of the market crashes the value by 40% overnight, wiping out their food budget. Is it ethical to onboard vulnerable populations onto high-risk financial tech?

You are designing a peer-to-peer payment app. The fraud detection AI flags transactions between strangers in rapid succession as suspicious. This pattern matches panhandling. The algorithm bans the accounts of homeless users relying on digital donations. Do you lower the fraud sensitivity, risking chargebacks, or keep the ban?

A company offers free 'Solar Kiosks' for charging phones in homeless encampments. In exchange, the kiosk harvests MAC addresses and browsing metadata from connected devices to sell to advertisers. The users have no other power source. Is this a fair trade or exploitation of desperation?

A homeless woman relies on an old smartphone for safety maps and emergency calls. The OS is no longer supported, and banking apps stop working. She cannot afford a new phone. You are a developer for the bank. Do you maintain a security-compromised legacy version of the app for users like her, or cut them off to protect the wider system?

Police regularly seize phones from homeless individuals during arrests, often keeping them for months as 'evidence.' You are asked to create a 'Remote Cloud Boot' feature that allows a user to access their phone's environment from a library computer. However, this feature could also be used by hackers to clone phones. Do you build it?

A 'Safety App' for the homeless allows users to broadcast their location to outreach workers during a crisis. However, the data is unencrypted. Abusive ex-partners or predators could intercept the signal to find the user. Do you release the app with weak security to get it out fast, or delay for months to encrypt it?

Public Wi-Fi in a city park restricts bandwidth and blocks streaming services to discourage 'loitering' by homeless youth who use it for entertainment and connection. You are the network admin. Do you bypass the throttle, knowing the city might shut down the Wi-Fi entirely if costs rise?

A phone recycling program distributes wiped corporate phones to the homeless. The phones are MDM (Mobile Device Management) locked, preventing the installation of unauthorized apps. The users cannot install games or social media, only 'approved' job-seeking apps. Is this charity or digital incarceration?

You develop a weather alert app. It sends high-decibel alarms for freezing conditions. For a homeless user hiding in a library or sleeping in a crowded shelter, the alarm causes them to be kicked out due to noise rules. Do you add a 'silent mode' that risks them sleeping through a freeze warning?

A homeless user's phone is their only storage for photos of deceased family. The phone is stolen. A 'Remote Wipe' command is standard security protocol. If they wipe it, they protect their identity but lose their memories. If they don't, they risk identity theft. How do you advise them?

You are training a predictive policing algorithm. The data shows high call volumes in areas with homeless encampments (often for nuisance calls, not violent crime). The model predicts these areas as 'High Crime Zones,' directing aggressive patrol units there. Do you filter out 'nuisance' calls, potentially missing real crime trends, or allow the algorithm to target the homeless?

A city installs 'Smart Streetlights' equipped with audio sensors to detect gunshots. The sensors also pick up aggressive shouting. The system automatically dispatches police to domestic arguments in tent cities, often escalating the situation rather than sending social workers. Do you disable the audio monitoring in those sectors?

Drones are used to map heat signatures in forests to prevent wildfires. They also identify hidden homeless camps. The forestry service wants to use this data to evict campers 'for their own safety.' As the drone operator, do you delete the footage of the camps?

A facial recognition system is deployed in a subway. It flags individuals with outstanding bench warrants (often for unpaid tickets or sleeping in public). This effectively bans homeless individuals with minor infractions from using public transport or seeking warmth. Do you implement the system?

Automated License Plate Readers (ALPR) scan for stolen cars. They also log vehicles that haven't moved in 72 hours, flagging people living in their cars for towing. You maintain the database. Do you create a 'grace period' algorithm for vehicle dwellers, or strictly enforce the code?

A risk assessment algorithm determines bail amounts. It uses 'stable address' as a heavy weighting factor for flight risk. This guarantees that homeless arrestees remain in jail while wealthier suspects go free. Do you remove the address variable, making the algorithm less accurate for flight risk, or keep it?

Robotic security dogs are deployed to patrol a private business district to 'deter vagrancy.' They film and broadcast live feeds of people sleeping on sidewalks. The manufacturer claims it reduces human-guard violence. Is the psychological terror of robotic surveillance a better alternative to physical removal?

A 'Citizen Reporting' app allows residents to snap photos of 'urban blight' (trash, graffiti, tents) to alert city services. The app gamifies this with points. Users begin competitively reporting homeless camps to clear the leaderboard, leading to daily sweeps. Do you remove the gamification elements, reducing user engagement, or keep the app as is?

An undocumented immigrant needs to access a municipal ID program to enroll children in school, but the database is hosted by a third-party vendor with a history of selling data to federal agencies. Do they risk the digital paper trail or keep their children out of the system?

A refugee from a war-torn region has digital scans of their university degree, but the physical university archives were burned. A credential verification startup demands the original metadata which was scrubbed for safety during transit. How do they prove their qualifications without the 'correct' digital forensics?

An asylum seeker is asked to use a biometric digital wallet to receive food aid in a camp. They know this biometric data is shared with the government they fled. Do they starve or surrender their biological identity to their persecutors?

A visa holder's status depends on a digital portal that frequently crashes and has no paper backup. They miss a renewal deadline due to a server error, but the logs show 'user inactivity.' How do they prove a system failure against an automated deportation trigger?

An undocumented person considers using a decentralized identity (blockchain) service to store health records, but the immutability of the ledger means they can never erase their location history if policies change. Is permanent proof worth permanent tracking?

A refugee uses a fake digital footprint to cross a border safely. Now, applying for legal status, they must submit social media history. Admitting the fake profile proves 'fraud,' but hiding it leaves gaps that look suspicious. Which truth gets them deported?

A tech platform offers free cloud storage for migrants to save copies of passports and birth certificates. The terms of service allow AI training on uploaded images. Does the user risk their documents being used to train the very facial recognition systems used to police borders?

A stateless person is offered a 'digital citizenship' from a micronation that allows them to open a bank account. However, using this ID flags them on international terror watchlists due to lack of recognition. Do they remain unbanked or risk being flagged as a threat?

A refugee wants to video call their parents in an occupied territory. The only reliable app is monitored by that regime. If they call, they expose their parents' location; if they don't, they may never say goodbye. Is silence the only safety?

An immigrant family uses a group chat to coordinate daily safety. One member is detained and their phone is seized. The group must decide whether to kick the member out and delete the chat (losing evidence of their safety check-ins) or risk the authorities reading the history.

A dissident in exile discovers their phone has spyware installed by their home country. They need to warn their network, but any message sent from the infected device will identify the recipients to the regime. How do they signal danger without becoming the beacon?

To get a visa, an applicant must register their social media handles. They have a private, anonymous account used to support LGBTQ+ rights—illegal in their home country. Do they declare it and risk persecution at home, or hide it and risk visa fraud charges?

A migrant worker uses a VPN to access news from home. The host country criminalizes VPN use for non-citizens as 'intent to conceal.' Do they stay informed and risk arrest, or remain ignorant and compliant?

An asylum seeker is advised to delete 'suspicious' contacts before a border check. However, these contacts are their only witnesses for their asylum case. Does the digital phonebook serve as evidence of persecution or grounds for inadmissibility?

A community relies on an encrypted messaging app. The app introduces a 'report spam' feature that forwards the last 5 messages to moderators. If a malicious actor reports a political discussion as spam, the encryption is broken for those messages. Do they trust the platform moderation?

A mother leaves a digital voice note for her child who is being smuggled separately. If the smuggler is caught, the voice note proves the mother 'endangered a minor' (a crime). If she doesn't send it, the child has no proof of who to trust. What is the digital cost of comfort?

An undocumented worker finds a gig app that doesn't require a Social Security Number, but it tracks GPS location 24/7. The employer sells this 'fleet data' to data brokers. Is the paycheck worth the real-time surveillance map of their life?

A construction site uses facial recognition for clock-ins to prevent 'buddy punching.' An undocumented worker knows their face is in a deportation database. If they scan, they risk a match; if they refuse, they are fired for 'non-compliance.' How do they work invisibly?

A visa holder is asked by their employer to train an AI model. They realize the model is being designed to automate their specific job category. If they refuse, they lose their sponsorship and must leave the country. Do they code their own obsolescence?

An immigrant delivery driver is constantly downrated by an algorithm for 'unexplained stops,' which are actually prayer breaks. They can't explain this to the app without flagging themselves as a religious minority in a hostile area. Do they stop praying or lose the job?

A domestic worker is required to download a 'smart home' app to manage their employer's house. The app records audio snippets to improve functionality. The worker knows these snippets could capture their conversations with family about their legal status. Do they accept the spy in their pocket?

A tech company recruits 'diverse' talent on H1-B visas but installs aggressive keystroke monitoring software on their laptops, unlike citizen employees. The workers fear that complaining about the privacy violation will be seen as 'rocking the boat' and jeopardize their renewal.

An undocumented person 'rents' a verified account on a gig platform to work. The account owner demands a higher cut or threatens to report them to authorities using the digital log of their work history. It's digital indentured servitude.

A skilled refugee coder is offered under-the-table crypto work for a DAO. The work is legitimate coding, but the payment method is flagged by financial regulators as 'high risk.' Cashing out could trigger a money laundering investigation they cannot survive legally.

An asylum seeker has video evidence of torture on their phone. Border agents demand the device password. If they refuse, the device is confiscated and they cannot access the evidence for their hearing. If they unlock it, agents might delete the file or contact the torturers found in the contacts.

AI-powered 'lie detection' kiosks are installed at the border to screen asylum claims. The AI flags the applicant's lack of eye contact (a cultural sign of respect in their home country) as 'deception.' Do they mimic Western body language and risk looking rehearsed, or act naturally and fail the algorithm?

To prove persecution, a refugee must provide Facebook posts where they criticized their government. However, Facebook's content moderation AI deleted those posts years ago for 'violating community standards on violence.' The digital proof of their danger has been sanitized away.

A witness to a war crime is in hiding. An international court wants their testimony via video link. The court cannot guarantee the video feed won't be intercepted by the regime's hackers. Does the witness speak and die, or stay silent and let the criminal walk?

An asylum seeker finds their story has been used in a 'viral' social media campaign by an NGO without their consent. The visibility helps their case but endangers their family back home who are now known targets. Do they demand the content be taken down and lose public support?

A lawyer suggests using a generative AI to translate an affidavit to save money. The AI hallucinates a detail about 'weapons' that wasn't in the original text. The error is caught, but the draft is in the cloud history. Could this hallucination be used to frame the applicant as a threat?

DNA testing is offered to prove a relationship for family reunification. The applicant knows the DNA data will be stored in a criminal forensics database. By reuniting their family, are they genetically framing their children as future suspects?

An applicant must turn over their cloud location history to prove they were in specific danger zones. The history also reveals the location of safe houses used by others still fleeing. Do they burn the safe house to save themselves?

A mutual aid group uses a public Venmo feed to distribute cash for rent. Immigration enforcement scrapes this public data to map the network of undocumented residents in a specific neighborhood. Does the group go back to cash (risky/slow) or expose their network?

A 'Know Your Rights' app records police interactions. It automatically uploads video to the cloud. If a user triggers it during a raid, the phone alerts the officers. Does the tool meant to protect them escalate the violence of the encounter?

Community organizers want to use a geofencing alert system to warn residents of ICE sightings. However, creating a database of subscribers effectively creates a 'deportation list' if the server is subpoenaed. How do they broadcast warnings without listing targets?

A religious center installs License Plate Readers (ALPR) for security after a hate crime. They realize the system shares data with local police, who share it with federal immigration. Do they keep the security system and endanger their undocumented congregants?

An immigrant rights group uses a popular event platform to organize protests. The platform updates its privacy policy to allow data sharing with 'government entities for national security.' Canceling the event kills momentum; continuing hands over the attendee list.

A neighborhood uses a private Nextdoor-style app. A well-meaning neighbor posts photos of 'suspicious vehicles' (unmarked law enforcement). The app algorithms flag the post as 'doxing law enforcement' and ban the user. The community loses its early warning system.

Crowdfunding is launched for a deportee's legal fees. The platform displays the full names of donors. Undocumented friends want to donate but fear their names appearing on a 'support network' list. The campaign fails to reach its goal due to fear of attribution.

During a pandemic, a city releases a contact tracing app that requires Bluetooth. Immigrant communities refuse to download it, fearing it tracks location for deportation. The community leaders must decide: encourage the app to save lives from the virus, or boycott it to save lives from deportation?

I'm working down in the Silicon Docks for one of the big lads, writing the algorithm that keeps people scrolling on the timeline. The engagement metrics are through the roof, fair play to us, but I'm after seeing my young niece at Sunday dinner glued to the screen, totally anxious, ignoring the family. It's my code doing that to her. Do I keep taking the massive salary to pay the rent in D4, or do I flag that we're actively breaking people's brains for ad revenue?

Your man from California flies in and tells us we need to train the AI on Irish language data to be inclusive. Grand idea, except he wants us to scrape everything from TG4 and the Gaeltacht archives without asking permission or paying a cent to the creators. It feels like digital colonialism, so it does. Do I build the scraper or tell him where to shove his 'inclusivity'?

The housing crisis in Dublin is fierce, and here I am coding a platform that helps landlords optimize short-term lets for tourists rather than long-term tenants. My own mates are emigrating because they can't find a place to live, and I'm basically automating their eviction. Is it enough to say 'it's just a tool', or am I part of the problem?

We're handling content moderation for the whole EU right here in Sandyford. The stuff I'm seeing would turn your stomach—absolute filth. We're under strict NDAs not to talk about it, but the mental health support is a joke—an app and a cup of tea. If I leak the working conditions to the papers, I'll be sued into oblivion, but if I stay quiet, the burnout is going to kill someone.

Sure look, the company is paying barely any tax here thanks to the 'Double Irish' legacy setups and IP shifting. I'm proud of the work we do, but when I walk past the homeless tents on the canal to get to our shiny glass office with free food, the guilt is eating me alive. Should I push for an internal CSR initiative, or is that just putting lipstick on a pig?

My team is developing facial recognition for 'security', but we know well it's going to be sold to regimes that aren't exactly democratic. The boss says, 'If we don't build it in Dublin, they'll build it in Shenzhen.' Is that a valid excuse to write code that could lock up protestors, or am I just washing my hands of it?

We're launching a new feature that tracks user location 'to improve service', but I know for a fact the data is being packaged and sold to insurers. It's technically legal under the Terms of Service nobody reads, but it feels fierce shady. Do I whistleblow to the Data Protection Commission and risk my career in this town?

The 'culture' in the office is all beanbags and free beer, but they're cracking down on anyone trying to unionize. They're monitoring our internal Slack channels for keywords like 'union' or 'representation'. I'm the admin with access to the logs. Do I warn the organizers they're being watched, or do I protect my own job and say nothing?

The National Broadband Plan has been 'coming soon' for donkey's years. I've a chance to set up a community mesh network using some grey-market gear to get the valley connected so the kids can do their homework. It's not strictly legal by ComReg standards, but the government has left us rotting. Do I break the law to get the village online?

I'm a farmer in Tipp, and these new automated tractors are grand, but John Deere locks the software so I can't fix it myself with a spanner anymore. I have to pay a technician a fortune to come out and press a button. Someone offered me a cracked firmware that lets me repair my own gear. Is it ethical to pirate the software of the tractor I own, just to keep the farm running?

The local pub is dying on its feet because everyone's at home on Netflix or scrolling TikTok. I'm developing an app to help rural pubs market themselves, but it relies on gamifying drinking—points for pints, essentially. Am I saving the community hub by encouraging alcoholism, or is the pub culture dead anyway?

My elderly mother is alone out in Connemara. I want to install a full sensor suite—cameras, motion detectors, the works—so I can watch her from Dublin. She says she hates the idea of being spied on, but she's had a fall before. Do I override her dignity for her safety, or leave her be and risk finding her too late?

A big tech crowd wants to test their delivery drones in our area because the airspace is empty. It'll bring a few jobs to the local hub, but the noise is driving the sheep mad and annoying the locals who moved here for the quiet. Do we take the foreign investment and lose the peace, or tell them to buzz off?

We're using AI to analyze soil samples to reduce fertilizer use, which is great for the environment. But the data goes straight to a multinational that's using it to buy up the most productive land, pushing out small family farms. I'm helping the environment but killing the community. What's the right move?

The GAA club wants to use a new app for managing the underage teams, but it demands a rake of data on the kids—location, health info, parents' details. I'm the only one on the committee who understands GDPR and sees the risk, but if I block it, I'm the eejit stopping the club from modernizing. Do I hold the line?

Tourism is the only thing keeping the town afloat, and Airbnb is driving it. But now, no local can afford to rent a house. I've built a bot that helps locals snatch up long-term rentals the second they go online, giving them an unfair advantage over the tourists. Is it fair to rig the market to save the village?

Living right on the border near Newry, and the police want to put up 'Smart Border' cameras that track every car crossing over. They say it's for catching smugglers, but given the history of this place, people are fierce paranoid about surveillance. I've been asked to consult on the tech. Do I help make it efficient, or refuse and let them build a botched system that might be worse?

Post-Brexit, the data sharing between the NHS in the North and the HSE in the South is a legal minefield. I have a patient who crosses the border daily. Do I share their medical file informally via encrypted email to ensure they get treatment, breaking the data laws, or stick to the protocol and risk their health?

I'm moderating a local community forum for a border town. The algorithms are flagging terms that are part of our daily vernacular as 'hate speech' because they don't understand the context, while missing actual sectarian dog-whistles. Do I train the AI on the slang, potentially teaching it how to be a better bigot, or keep doing it manually and drowning in the toxicity?

A company wants to map the 'Peace Walls' in Belfast for a mixed-reality history tour app. It sounds grand, educational. But locals are worried it'll turn their trauma into a theme park for tourists and maybe even identify homes of people who want to stay anonymous. Is some history better left un-digitized?

With the different regulations now, I can route our company's user data through a server in Belfast to bypass some strict Dublin EU rules, or vice versa. It's a legal grey area—the 'digital border' is porous. It saves the company millions. Am I a cute hoor for spotting the loophole, or undermining the law?

The PSNI (Police Service of Northern Ireland) had that massive data breach where officers' names were leaked. I run a cybersecurity firm and I've found a copy of the list on the dark web. Do I buy it to secure it and hand it over, knowing I'm funding the criminals, or leave it out there where paramilitaries might find it?

We're building a genealogy app, and in the border counties, DNA tests are bringing up secrets about who's related to who from the Troubles era. It's causing unmerciful rows and distress. Should we suppress matches that suggest 'non-paternal events' in this specific region to keep the peace, or is the truth the truth?

Drones are being used to monitor illegal dumping and diesel smuggling along the border. The locals are shooting them down, saying it's spy gear. I supply the drones. Do I arm them with better tracking and altitude capabilities to outsmart the locals, or accept that in border country, surveillance is an act of aggression?

We're building another massive data center on the outskirts of Dublin. The grid is creaking; we've been told there might be brownouts this winter for regular houses, but our contract guarantees us power 24/7. Is it right to keep the servers cool for TikTok videos while Mrs. Murphy down the road might lose her heating?

A tech giant wants to build a data center in a rural area, promising construction jobs. But once it's built, it'll employ about ten people and consume the water of a medium-sized town. The council is broke and needs the rates (taxes). Do I vote to approve it for the short-term cash, knowing it's a long-term parasite?

I manage the cooling systems. We could run them hotter to save energy—the servers can take it—but it increases the risk of a crash by 0.5%. Management says '100% uptime' is the god we worship. Do I secretly adjust the setpoints to save megawatts of power, hoping nobody notices?

We're offsetting our carbon emissions by planting trees, but not in Ireland—we're buying cheap credits in South America. Meanwhile, our diesel generators in Clondalkin are running full tilt during peak hours. It's greenwashing, pure and simple. Do I sign off on the sustainability report?

There's a proposal to hook the data center's waste heat into a district heating system for a new housing estate. Sounds brilliant, but it locks those houses into dependency on the tech company. If the company leaves or upgrades the tech, the heating goes. Is it a symbiotic relationship or a hostage situation?

The planning permission requires us to protect the local biodiversity. There's a badger sett right where the backup generator needs to go. My boss says, 'Sure, they're nocturnal, move them at night and nobody will know.' Do I report the violation and delay a billion-euro project, or let the badgers take one for the digital economy?

We're storing data for countries with terrible human rights records because Ireland is considered a 'safe haven'. The servers are physically here, protected by Irish law, but the data is being used to oppress people abroad. Are we complicit by providing the digital vault?

Local residents are protesting the noise of the fans. We can build sound baffles, but they're expensive and reduce efficiency. The legal limit allows the noise, but it's wrecking the neighbours' sleep. Do strictly follow the law, or do the decent thing and spend the money to be a good neighbour?

Sure look, the Data Protection Commission (DPC) is swamped. I'm working there, and I have a file on a massive breach by a US tech giant that affects millions. But I've been told to prioritize 'amicable resolution' because the government is terrified of the multinationals pulling out of Dublin. Do I bury the file or leak it to Max Schrems?

I'm a consultant advising small Irish businesses. A local GAA club keeps a spreadsheet of members' details on an unsecured laptop. Strictly speaking, I should report them or force them to buy expensive software they can't afford. Do I turn a blind eye because 'it's only the lads', or enforce the law?

The 'One Stop Shop' mechanism means Ireland regulates for the whole EU. Other European regulators are raging at us, saying we're too soft. I'm in a meeting where we're discussing a fine that's pocket change to the company. If I speak up and say it's too low, I'm 'anti-business'. If I don't, I'm failing 400 million Europeans. What's the craic?

We're designing a 'consent cookie' banner. The client wants the 'Reject All' button to be grey and hidden in a submenu, while 'Accept All' is bright green. It's technically compliant but manipulative—'dark patterns', they call it. Do I design it to trick my own granny, or insist on a fair interface?

A US company is threatening to move 500 jobs to Switzerland if the DPC enforces a strict interpretation of data transfer rules. I'm a civil servant; my job is to protect Irish interests. Is protecting Irish jobs more important than the abstract privacy rights of a German citizen?

I have access to the 'Right to be Forgotten' requests. A local politician wants links to an old scandal removed. It's in the public interest, but he's arguing it's 'outdated and irrelevant'. If I approve it, I'm helping him sanitize his past before an election. If I refuse, he'll make my life hell. What do I do?

We're implementing age verification for an Irish social media site to protect kids. But to do it, we need users to upload passports or IDs, creating a massive honeypot of identity data. We're trading privacy for safety. Is it worth the risk of that database getting hacked?

The EU is demanding we fine a company billions. The fines go to the Irish exchequer, which sounds grand, but it makes us look like we're profiteering from enforcement. The company is offering a settlement that includes building a new park and community centre in Dublin 4. Do we take the bribe—sorry, the 'settlement'—or the fine?

A dating app for gay men discovers a vulnerability that exposes user location data. In countries where homosexuality is punishable by death, patching the flaw requires a server downtime that might alert authorities to the app's traffic patterns. How do developers balance transparency with the immediate physical danger to users in hostile regimes?

A ride-sharing algorithm matches a trans woman with a driver who has a history of posting transphobic content on linked social media, but no criminal record. Should the platform use off-platform behavior to filter driver-rider matches to prevent potential hate crimes, or does this violate driver privacy?

Smart home security cameras use facial recognition to identify 'strangers.' A user's closeted partner is repeatedly flagged as a security threat to the user's family members who have access to the feed. How should the system handle frequent visitors without forcing an outing of the relationship?

An encrypted messaging app identifies a ring of users entraping LGBTQ+ individuals in a region with anti-sodomy laws. Banning the attackers alerts them to change tactics; leaving them active risks more victims. What is the ethical intervention strategy?

A travel safety app aggregates crime data to warn tourists. It flags LGBTQ+ neighborhoods as 'high risk' due to higher rates of hate crimes, inadvertently discouraging tourism and hurting queer-owned businesses while potentially guiding hate groups to these areas.

Police request data from a fitness tracker to solve a murder. The data inadvertently reveals the user's attendance at an underground LGBTQ+ venue in a jurisdiction where such gatherings are illegal. Does the platform comply with the warrant or protect the user's civil rights at the risk of legal obstruction?

A digital wallet feature allows users to easily split bills. The public transaction feed reveals a pattern of payments between two closeted individuals, which is scraped by a third party for blackmail. How should financial social features be designed to prevent pattern-of-life analysis?

An autonomous vehicle is programmed to prioritize passenger safety. If a trans passenger is attacked by a mob blocking the road, does the AI have the ethical clearance to drive through the crowd, potentially injuring aggressors, to save the passenger?

A retail store uses AI to estimate customer demographics for ad targeting. The system repeatedly misgenders a non-binary customer on digital displays, causing public humiliation and dysphoria. Is the efficiency of targeted ads worth the psychological harm of automated misgendering?

A banking system's legacy code requires a legal name change to update user profiles. A trans user has socially transitioned but cannot afford the legal process, resulting in constant dead-naming by support staff and ATMs. How much technical debt is acceptable when it causes active psychological harm?

A social media platform's 'Real Name' policy is intended to reduce trolling but disproportionately suspends drag performers and trans people who use chosen names. How does a platform balance accountability with the right to self-identification?

Voice recognition software for banking fails to authenticate a trans woman because her voice pitch does not match the 'female' baseline in the training data. Should the system lower security thresholds for voice variance or require invasive retraining?

A memorialization AI scrapes social media to create avatars of deceased users. It recreates a trans person using pre-transition photos and their deadname because that data is more voluminous historically. Who owns the digital memory of a person's identity?

A video game character creator locks customization options (clothing, hair, voice) to binary biological sex choices to 'prevent clipping issues.' This excludes non-binary players. Is technical optimization a valid excuse for exclusionary design?

Biometric airport scanners flag trans travelers for 'anomalies' because their body topography doesn't match the gender marker selected by the TSA agent. This leads to invasive pat-downs. How should security hardware be redesigned to respect bodily autonomy?

An employment screening AI penalizes resumes with pronouns listed (e.g., they/them) based on historical hiring data that favors cisnormative candidates. How do engineers de-bias a model that is accurately reflecting societal bias?

An Electronic Health Record (EHR) system automatically shares a patient's full medical history with all treating specialists. A trans man visiting a podiatrist is outed regarding his gynecological history, leading to discrimination. How should data granularity be managed in interoperable health systems?

A period tracking app sells anonymized aggregate data to researchers. In a political climate where abortion and gender-affirming care are criminalized, this data could be de-anonymized to prosecute trans men or non-binary people. Is retaining this data ethical?

Social media ad algorithms identify a user as 'likely LGBTQ+' and serve ads for conversion therapy services labeled as 'spiritual counseling.' The platform claims neutrality in ad delivery. At what point does algorithmic targeting become complicity in psychological abuse?

An AI therapist is trained on general CBT principles but lacks specific training on gender dysphoria. It suggests 'body acceptance' techniques to a trans teen that mirror conversion therapy rhetoric, worsening their distress. Should general-purpose AI be restricted from handling specialized mental health topics?

A telemedicine platform operates in a state that bans gender-affirming care. The platform's encryption prevents law enforcement from seeing patient data, but the company is subpoenaed for provider metadata. Complying exposes doctors; refusing risks the platform's shutdown.

A genetic testing service reveals 'biological sex' results that contradict a user's lived gender identity to their family members via a 'ancestry sharing' feature. How should genetic privacy account for social identity?

An insurance algorithm automatically denies coverage for facial feminization surgery, categorizing it as 'cosmetic' based on cisnormative standards, despite medical consensus on its necessity for treating dysphoria. How do we audit algorithms for medical necessity bias?

A pharmacy app sends push notifications including medication names. A notification for HIV antiretrovirals (PrEP) appears on a user's lock screen, visible to their conservative colleagues. How should privacy UI/UX differ for stigmatized healthcare?

A content moderation AI flags terms like 'dyke' or 'queer' as hate speech, resulting in the suspension of LGBTQ+ activists reclaiming these slurs. Meanwhile, coded homophobic dog-whistles evade detection. How can NLP systems understand community context versus hate speech?

A recommendation algorithm notices a user interacting with trans-positive content and begins suggesting 'debate' videos from anti-trans influencers to maximize engagement through outrage. Is maximizing 'time on site' ethically viable when it relies on radicalization pipelines?

To prevent catfishing, a queer dating app requires photo verification. This excludes closeted individuals who cannot risk having a face picture on file, as well as those with dysmorphia. How do digital spaces balance trust with accessibility for the marginalized?

An automated filter blocks 'sexual content' to comply with app store guidelines. This results in the removal of non-sexual educational content about safe sex for gay men, effectively censoring health information. Who decides the line between 'adult content' and 'community health'?

A crowdfunding platform suspends a fundraiser for gender-affirming surgery because the user's legal name on their bank account doesn't match their campaign identity, flagging it as fraud. How can financial tech accommodate name fluidity?

A generative AI model refuses to write a story about a same-sex romance, citing 'content safety policies' regarding sexually explicit material, yet readily writes similar hetero-normative romance stories. How does 'safety' alignment become erasure?

A virtual reality social space allows users to block avatars they find 'annoying.' Organized groups use this to mass-block trans users, effectively erasing them from the public digital square. Is the right to curate one's feed superior to the right of others to exist in public spaces?

An event platform automatically categorizes Drag Story Hour events as 'Political/Controversial,' removing them from general family-friendly search results. Does algorithmic categorization enforce cultural segregation?

School web filtering software blocks access to LGBTQ+ suicide prevention resources under the category 'Alternative Lifestyles,' while allowing access to religious sites condemning homosexuality. Does the school's duty of care extend to digital information access?

A parental monitoring app uses AI to analyze a teenager's text messages. It flags keywords related to coming out and alerts the parents, who are abusive. Does the child's right to safety override the parent's right to supervise?

An educational platform allows students to set their preferred pronouns. A software update creates a 'parent portal' that automatically displays these preferences to guardians without the student's consent, potentially outing them. How should student data privacy be architected?

A social media algorithm's 'People You May Know' feature suggests a closeted LGBTQ+ youth's secret profile to their family members based on location and IP overlap. How can platforms prevent graph-based outing?

A smart toy records children's questions to improve its conversational AI. A child asks the toy about gender feelings they haven't shared with anyone. This audio is stored on a cloud server accessible to employees for QA. Is this a violation of the child's future privacy?

A library e-book system tracks reading history. A teen checks out several LGBTQ+ themed books. The system's 'year in review' email, sent to the family's shared account, highlights these genres. How should shared family accounts handle individual privacy?

An anti-bullying AI in a game chat fails to detect misgendering because it doesn't view pronouns as 'insults,' leaving trans youth exposed to harassment while penalizing them for snapping back at bullies.

Online proctoring software flags a neurodivergent trans student for 'suspicious behavior' (stimming) and mismatching ID photos (pre-transition), potentially failing them. How do we ensure academic integrity tools don't discriminate against intersectional identities?

An auto parts plant in Toledo installs 'productivity wearables' that track arm movements to the millisecond. The data shows that an older, beloved shift foreman is 15% slower than the new hires, but his error rate is zero. The algorithm automatically flags him for a 'performance improvement plan' that is the first step to termination. Do you override the system?

A union organizer in a Michigan stamping plant discovers that management is using heat-mapping data from the factory Wi-Fi to identify where workers congregate for more than 3 minutes, effectively predicting and breaking up union talks before they start. Is this a safety measure or illegal surveillance?

A Kenosha logistics center implements an AI scheduling system that maximizes efficiency but systematically schedules single mothers for 'flex shifts' that make childcare impossible to secure. The company claims the algorithm is 'gender neutral' based purely on demand availability.

A historic steel mill in Ohio introduces 'Cobots' (collaborative robots) to work alongside humans. The sensors record every conversation within a 10-foot radius 'for training purposes.' Workers realize the recordings are being accessed by HR to adjudicate disputes in the breakroom.

During a severe blizzard in Minnesota, a warehouse algorithm automatically fires 15 employees for failing to meet pick-rates because delivery trucks couldn't arrive. The local manager knows reinstatement requires a corporate appeal process that takes weeks, leaving families without pay in winter.

A manufacturing company offers free Fitbits to lower health insurance premiums for workers. It turns out the data is being sold to a third-party actuary to adjust rates for the entire county based on the aggregate health of the workforce, penalizing the whole town.

An Indiana RV manufacturer uses eye-tracking cameras to monitor driver fatigue in their delivery fleet. The system flags drivers who wear prescription bifocals as 'distracted' due to head tilt, threatening the jobs of the most experienced drivers.

A gig-economy delivery platform enters a mid-sized Wisconsin city, undercutting local courier services. They refuse to share the data on how 'surge pricing' is calculated, leading local drivers to suspect the algorithm is artificially inflating prices to kill off local competition before raising rates.

A third-generation Iowa corn farmer fixes a sensor on his tractor himself to beat the rain. The manufacturer's software detects the 'unauthorized repair' and bricks the tractor remotely during harvest. He has to hack his own equipment to save the crop.

A seed conglomerate offers free precision-ag software to Minnesota soybean farmers. The fine print says the company owns the yield data. They use this data to buy up the most productive land in the county through shell companies, outbidding the local families who generated the data.

A dairy co-op implements automated milking machines. The vendor requires a permanent internet connection to 'optimize' the milk flow. When the rural broadband goes down for three days, the machines lock out, causing a health crisis for the herd.

Drone surveillance by a major ag-tech firm flies over private fields in Illinois to detect if farmers are saving patented seeds from the previous year. A farmer shoots down a drone hovering over his house, claiming privacy violation; the company sues for destruction of property.

An AI pricing model for a regional grain elevator sets prices based on global futures and local satellite imagery. It predicts a neighbor's crop failure before he knows it, offering him a predatory low price for his remaining yield. Do you warn him?

Soil sensors placed by a university extension program identify a rare mineral deposit on a struggling family farm. The data is technically public. Do researchers publish it, knowing mining companies will pressure the family to sell their heritage?

A vertical farming startup in Chicago wants to partner with rural farmers for 'carbon credits,' paying them to not plant certain fields. The contract requires installing sensors that track all movement on the property to verify compliance, effectively surveilling the farm family's daily life.

Cattle electronic ear tags are introduced to track disease. The database is hacked, and the specific location and value of prize winning herds are leaked to a ring of cattle rustlers targeting high-value livestock in the Dakotas.

A national telecom provider refuses to run fiber to a 'hollow' in West Virginia/Ohio border because the ROI algorithm says the population density is too low. The town wants to build its own municipal broadband, but the telecom lobbies the state legislature to ban community-owned ISPs.

The only local newspaper in a Michigan county is bought by a hedge fund and replaced by an AI that scrapes police blotters to generate 'news.' The AI publishes an arrest record for a man who was later exonerated, destroying his reputation in the small town.

A 'Smart City' grant offers a Rust Belt town free pothole repair in exchange for installing streetlights with facial recognition cameras. The town council needs the road money but fears turning Main Street into a surveillance state.

A tight-knit neighborhood uses a Ring camera network. The footage is automatically shared with police without a warrant. A neighbor's camera catches a teen sneaking out for a secret relationship, and the 'community safety' group exposes them, causing a family crisis.

A Wisconsin tourist town is hollowed out by an algorithm used by property investors to buy up starter homes for Airbnb rentals. The algorithm predicts which houses will list before they hit the market, making it impossible for locals to buy homes.

A library in a conservative district is pressured to install filtering software to protect children. The software's 'obscenity' filter automatically blocks health sites regarding breast cancer and LGBTQ support groups, cutting off vital information for isolated residents.

An app designed to report 'suspicious activity' in a suburb becomes a hub for racial profiling against delivery drivers and utility workers. The moderator, a respected community elder, refuses to delete the posts, citing 'free speech' and 'neighborhood watch' traditions.

A utility company installs smart meters that can detect specific appliance usage. They use this data to fine residents for using space heaters during peak hours, disproportionately affecting the elderly who can't afford to upgrade their insulation.

A rural church adopts an online tithing app. The app developer sells the donor list to political action committees, and congregants start receiving targeted attack ads based on their donation amounts. The pastor feels he betrayed his flock's trust.

During a livestreamed funeral service, the platform's copyright bot mutes the audio because the choir sang a copyrighted hymn. The remote family members miss the eulogy. Does the church break the law to pirate the stream for the next service?

A youth pastor uses a location-tracking app for a teen retreat 'for safety.' He forgets to turn it off after the trip and inadvertently tracks a teen visiting a Planned Parenthood clinic. He now faces a dilemma of confidentiality vs. parental notification.

An aging congregation installs facial recognition to help the new pastor remember names. The system starts logging attendance and automatically sends 'we missed you' emails to absentees, making the church feel like a debt collector rather than a community.
A mega-church moves into a small town and uses 'geofencing' to target ads to phones inside the historic local chapels on Sunday mornings. The local pastors view this as digital sheep-stealing.

A pastor admits to using ChatGPT to write his sermons because he is burned out visiting sick parishioners. The sermons are popular, but the deacons feel the 'Holy Spirit' has been outsourced to an algorithm.

A church runs a digital 'prayer wall.' A scraper bot harvests the names and health struggles posted by members to build profiles for scam callers claiming to be hospital administrators demanding payment.

An Amish community is pressured by the state to install digital turn signals on their buggies for safety on high-speed roads. They refuse on religious grounds, but the data shows a 40% reduction in accidents with the tech. How does the state balance safety vs. religious freedom?

A rural school district accepts free Chromebooks that require Google account tracking. The only internet access for many students is a 4G hotspot that filters content. A student researching hunting rifles for a 4-H project is flagged as a 'violence risk' and suspended.

To save money on busing, a district uses an algorithm to optimize routes. The new route forces farm kids to be on the bus for 2 hours each way, meaning they can't do chores. The algorithm says it's 'optimal,' but the family farm economy relies on that labor.

An AI grading system is implemented to help overworked teachers. It consistently marks down essays written in AAVE (African American Vernacular English) or rural dialects as 'grammatically poor,' forcing students to code-switch to pass, erasing their cultural voice.

A high school football team in Ohio uses biometric helmet sensors to track impact. The star quarterback takes a hit that registers as a concussion risk, but he feels fine. The coach wants to override the sensor to win the state championship game.

A school implements 'E-Learning Days' for snow days. 30% of the students live in areas with no broadband. The school suggests they sit in the McDonald's parking lot to do homework. Is this an equitable education policy?

A third-party lunch payment system tracks what students eat. They propose selling this data to the parents' health insurance providers to 'incentivize healthy choices,' effectively raising premiums for families who rely on the cheaper, processed school lunch options.

A wealthy suburban district donates their old iPads to a poor rural district. The iPads are still locked to the donor's management system, meaning the rural admin can't install local apps. The donor district refuses to unlock them citing 'security policies.'

Classroom management software allows teachers to view the screens of students at all times. A teacher notices a student is writing a suicide note in a private Google Doc during class. Does she intervene immediately, revealing she was spying, or follow standard counseling protocol?

A tribe wants to digitize their membership rolls and genealogy records to speed up enrollment verification. However, the most affordable cloud hosting provider stores data on servers subject to US federal subpoenas. The Tribal Council fears another era of federal surveillance or blood quantum auditing. Do they build expensive, slower on-reservation servers or risk data sovereignty for efficiency?

A major university proposes an 'Open Data' partnership to analyze reservation economic trends. The findings could bring grant money, but the raw data would become public domain. Indigenous Data Sovereignty principles assert the tribe must own the data, but the university policy requires open access. How does the tribe negotiate the need for funding against the risk of deficit-framing statistics?

A tech company offers to install fiber optics across a rural reservation in exchange for rights to the spectrum data and user metadata. The reservation currently has 40% connectivity. Is access to the modern world worth signing away the 'digital treaty rights' of the next generation?

Tribal law enforcement uses a shared federal database for criminal background checks. They discover the federal system is flagging tribal members based on participation in pipeline protests, labeling them 'extremists.' Does the tribe disconnect from the shared network and lose critical crime-fighting tools, or remain complicit in the surveillance of their own water protectors?

A blockchain startup approaches a tribe with a proposal to manage treaty annuity payments via cryptocurrency to bypass federal bureaucracy. However, the immutable ledger would permanently record financial transactions of members. Does the benefit of bypassing the BIA (Bureau of Indian Affairs) outweigh the privacy risks of an immutable public ledger?

State voter ID laws require a physical address, but many reservation homes use non-standard descriptions. A GIS mapping firm offers to 'formalize' the addresses for the state database. Elders worry this mapping is a prelude to taxation or land seizure. How do you balance the right to vote with the refusal to be mapped by an outside power?

An AI governance system is proposed to manage tribal housing waitlists to remove accusations of nepotism. The algorithm prioritizes 'need' based on western metrics (income, credit score) rather than traditional kinship obligations (housing extended family). Does adopting the 'unbiased' tool destroy the cultural social safety net?

A tribe asserts that their data sovereignty extends to genetic data held by commercial ancestry testing companies (e.g., 23andMe). They demand the deletion of all data linked to their specific genetic markers. The companies argue the individuals consented. Does the collective right of the tribe to control its identity supersede the individual consumer's contract?

A large language model (LLM) has scraped the internet and ingested stories that are culturally restricted—only to be told in winter or by specific clans. The AI is now generating these stories on demand. The tribe demands the model 'unlearn' this data. Is it possible to enforce cultural protocols on a neural network that has already processed the text?

A museum agrees to digitally repatriate sacred masks by providing high-resolution 3D scans to the tribe before destroying the physical copies or returning them. However, the museum wants to keep the digital files for 'educational purposes.' If the physical object was too sacred for public view, is the digital twin also restricted, or does it exist outside spiritual law?

Augmented Reality (AR) developers want to create a historical overlay for a National Park that sits on sacred tribal land. They want to show 'historical ceremonies.' The tribe objects, saying those ceremonies are not for tourists. The developers argue the land is public property and they have a First Amendment right to digital expression. Who owns the digital layer over sacred ground?

An elder agrees to record specific ceremonial songs for preservation, but stipulates they must strictly be accessed by tribal members. The archivist dies, and the files are found on a cloud drive with uncertain permissions. Does the tribe delete the only recording of the song to ensure protocol is kept, or risk the files leaking to save the knowledge?

AI image generators are creating 'Native American style' art that mimics specific sacred patterns used in healing rites. These images are being sold as NFTs. The patterns are not copyrighted under US law but are protected under tribal customary law. How does the tribe fight algorithmic appropriation of spiritual intellectual property?

Researchers want to use DNA from ancient ancestors found on tribal land to map migration patterns. The tribe believes disturbing the ancestors digitally (sequencing) is as violent as disturbing them physically. The scientists argue the knowledge belongs to humanity. Does scientific curiosity override the spiritual right to rest?

A video game studio wants to use accurate photogrammetry of a sacred mountain for a game level. They offer royalty payments to the tribe. The youth council wants the funding for a language program; the elders council says the mountain cannot be 'played on' virtually. Does virtual interaction constitute desecration?

A digital archive of oral histories includes voices of people who have passed away. In this tribe's tradition, viewing images or hearing voices of the dead is taboo for a year after death. How does the database manage 'digital death protocols' automatically without erasing history?

A mining company uses satellite imagery and machine learning to prospect for lithium (needed for green tech) on treaty lands without stepping foot on the ground. They claim this is legal remote sensing. The tribe claims this is 'digital trespassing' leading to resource extraction. At what point does data collection become a violation of territory?

To monitor climate change, scientists want to install sensors in a remote, sacred watershed. The data would help prove the tribe's water rights case in court. However, the sensors transmit real-time location data that poachers could use to find endangered species the tribe protects. Do you secure the legal right to water or the physical safety of the relatives (animals)?

A pipeline company uses drones to monitor their infrastructure crossing tribal land. The drones also capture high-res footage of backyard ceremonies and community gatherings. The company refuses to blur the footage, citing security needs. How does the tribe enforce privacy laws in the airspace above their sovereign soil?

Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK) regarding fire management is fed into a federal AI model for wildfire prevention. The AI suggests controlled burns in areas the tribe knows are spiritually volatile, but the model ignores 'spiritual' parameters. If the tribe withholds TEK, the forest burns; if they share it, it is misused. What is the path?

Smart meters are installed on reservation homes to improve energy efficiency. The data reveals exactly when families are home, their occupancy levels, and poverty levels (based on usage). The utility company sells this 'anonymized' data. The tribe wants to build its own utility to stop the data hemorrhage but lacks the capital. Is energy sovereignty a prerequisite for data privacy?

A mapping app directs tourists through a reservation to avoid traffic, leading to congestion on fragile dirt roads not meant for heavy use. The tribe asks the tech company to remove the routes; the company claims their algorithm simply finds the fastest public road. Does an algorithm have a responsibility to physical infrastructure integrity?

Agricultural tech companies want to test genetically modified seeds on reservation land, promising drought resistance. They require the tribe to sign data agreements sharing all soil and yield data. The tribe fears this data will be used to patent their indigenous corn varieties. How to accept food security tools without enabling biopiracy?

The tribe is offered a contract to host a massive data center. It would bring revenue, but the cooling systems require millions of gallons of water from the tribe's aquifer. Is it ethical to trade the water of future generations to store the data of the current one?

A 'Big Tech' company offers to build a high-quality translation model for an endangered Indigenous language. In return, they own the model and the training data. The tribe gets to use it for free, but they cannot modify it or stop the company from selling it to the military. Is saving the language worth losing ownership of it?

A tribe creates a private app to teach their language, restricting access to members to prevent outsiders from commodifying it. A hacker cracks the app and posts the dictionary online, claiming 'information wants to be free.' How does the tribe navigate the conflict between Western open-source ideals and Indigenous knowledge protection?

To train a speech recognition model, a tribe needs thousands of hours of audio. The only available source is old recordings of boarding school survivors telling traumatic stories. Is it ethical to feed the trauma of ancestors into a machine to save the language they were beaten for speaking?

An AI translator consistently translates a gender-neutral Indigenous pronoun into 'He' in English, reinforcing patriarchy. The tribe wants to fix the bias, but the 'black box' nature of the AI makes it difficult to pinpoint why. Do they abandon the tool or accept a colonized version of their language?

A tribe considers using synthetic voice technology to clone the voice of the last fluent speaker (with her consent before passing) to create new learning materials. Traditionalists argue that the 'breath of life' cannot be synthesized and that a machine speaking the language is a mockery. Is a robotic fluent teacher better than no teacher?

Language revitalization funding is tied to 'measurable outcomes.' A grant requires the tribe to use a specific app that tracks student progress and sends data to the federal government. The tribe worries this data will be used to justify cutting funding if progress is 'too slow' by Western standards.

Non-indigenous hobbyists are using AI to learn the language and are now producing 'fluent' content on YouTube that contains subtle cultural errors. They are drowning out the actual tribal teachers in search rankings. Does the tribe assert copyright over the language itself to stop the misinformation?

A keyboard app developed for the tribe's unique orthography also collects keystroke data to 'improve prediction.' The developer is a third-party non-native ally. Who owns the predictive text model derived from the collective thought-patterns of the tribe?

The Indian Health Service (IHS) migrates patient records to a new centralized national system. While secure, it allows data mining for 'population health' studies by federal researchers. Given the history of non-consensual sterilization and experimentation, can the tribe opt out of the national system without losing federal healthcare funding?

A pharmaceutical company wants to screen the tribe's unique microbiome to find cures for diabetes. They promise free medication for life. The tribe remembers the Havasupai case where blood samples were used for unrelated mental health research. How to structure a 'dynamic consent' model where the tribe controls the data for every single query?

Traditional healers are asked to input their patient interactions into an Electronic Health Record (EHR) to coordinate with medical doctors. The healers refuse, saying the specific plant mixtures and prayers cannot be written down in a government database. How to integrate care systems without digitizing (and exposing) proprietary medicinal knowledge?

Telehealth is the only option for a remote village, but the platform's Terms of Service state that video data can be reviewed by AI for 'quality assurance.' This means ceremonies performed during healing sessions are being watched by algorithms. Does the tribe demand a custom, unmonitored server, or forgo the service?

An AI mental health chatbot is deployed to address high suicide rates on the reservation. The bot is trained on Western psychology and fails to recognize 'historical trauma' or spiritual distress, frequently mislabeling users as psychotic. Is a culturally incompetent tool better than the total absence of mental health care?

A study proposes using wearable trackers to monitor physical activity of diabetic elders. The data shows elders walking 'off path' into restricted wilderness areas to harvest medicine. If this data is subpoenaed by land management agencies, the elders could be fined. Does the tribe ban the trackers to protect the harvesters?

Genomic researchers discover a gene variant in the tribe that protects against a specific heart disease. They want to patent a drug based on it. The tribe believes their DNA is not a 'resource' to be mined. If they refuse to participate, the researchers say they will just find the gene in urban tribal members who live off-reservation and don't answer to the tribal council.

To combat the fentanyl crisis, the tribal police want to use facial recognition and license plate readers at the reservation borders. Community members argue this turns the reservation into an open-air prison, mimicking the colonial containment of the past. Is internal surveillance acceptable if it protects the community from external threats?

An HR platform uses 'micro-expression analysis' during video interviews to screen for 'honesty and engagement,' automatically disqualifying autistic candidates who avoid eye contact or have flat affect.
A retail chain deploys anti-theft AI that flags 'erratic movement patterns' as suspicious, repeatedly detaining customers with Tourette's or those who stim for self-regulation.
A health insurance provider purchases data from voice-assistant companies to detect 'vocal biomarkers' of depression or bipolar onset, raising premiums before a diagnosis is ever sought.

Schools implement passive audio surveillance in hallways to detect 'aggressive tones,' resulting in disciplinary records for neurodivergent students whose natural volume or tone regulation differs from the norm.
A gaming platform's toxicity filter uses AI to auto-ban users for 'disruptive speech,' failing to distinguish between abusive language and vocal tics.
Social media algorithms infer an unconfirmed ADHD diagnosis based on scroll speed and watch time, selling this 'impulse control' profile to predatory loan advertisers.
Law enforcement uses predictive policing software that flags high-energy public behavior (mania or stimming) as 'pre-crime' agitation, leading to escalated confrontations.
A parenting app analyzes infant cooing and movement to predict autism risk, sharing the probability score with private preschools that then deny admission.
Remote proctoring software flags a student for 'cheating' because their eyes darted away from the screen to process information (a common ADHD/Autistic thinking trait).
An adaptive learning platform forces a linear progression of concepts, locking out students with dyslexia or dyscalculia who learn best through holistic or non-linear exploration.
Classroom management apps gamify behavior by displaying 'compliance scores' on a smartboard, publicly shaming students experiencing sensory overload or meltdowns.
A university mandates 'attention tracking' headbands that measure brainwaves, penalizing students whose focus style (hyperfocus vs. drift) doesn't match the neurotypical model.
Writing assistant AI aggressively corrects 'tangential' or 'complex' sentence structures, effectively erasing the unique creative voice of neurodivergent writers in favor of standardized simplicity.
A school district uses biometric wristbands to track 'emotional regulation,' sending automated alerts to parents whenever a child's heart rate spikes due to excitement or anxiety.
Virtual Reality social skills training simulations force autistic students to practice maintaining eye contact to 'win' the scenario, prioritizing masking over genuine communication.
AI-graded oral exams penalize pauses, stuttering, or non-standard pacing, disadvantaging students with apraxia or processing speed differences.
Productivity tracking software logs 'idle time' for any pause over 30 seconds, punishing ADHD workers who work in high-intensity bursts followed by recovery periods.
An AI 'tone checker' in Slack/Teams flags direct, concise communication styles common among autistic employees as 'hostile' or 'passive-aggressive' to HR.
Office 'smart lighting' and noise-masking systems are optimized for the average worker but create a sensory hell for those with sensory processing disorder, with no manual override.
A company uses AI to analyze meeting transcripts, consistently rating employees who don't speak during brainstorming sessions (but contribute later via text) as 'low value'.
Gig economy algorithms punish delivery drivers for taking 'inefficient' routes that avoid sensory-overwhelming traffic or construction zones.
A mandatory corporate wellness app tracks sleep and activity, flagging employees with 'irregular' circadian rhythms (common in ADHD/Bipolar) as high-risk or unreliable.
AI-driven personality tests for hiring filter out candidates with 'obsessive' attention to detail or 'rigid' thinking, systematically excluding OCD talent.
Wearable badges track 'social cohesion' by measuring how often employees speak to each other, penalizing those who need solitude to recharge or work effectively.
A dating app algorithm deprioritizes profiles that use vocabulary associated with 'special interests' or 'infodumping,' labeling them as low-quality interactions.
Social media platforms optimize for 'doomscrolling' by specifically targeting the dopamine-seeking loops of ADHD brains, making disengagement physiologically painful.
AR glasses with 'emotional overlay' misinterpret the facial expressions of a neurodivergent user's partner, advising the user that the partner is 'angry' when they are simply focused.
An AI 'communication coach' plugin rewrites a user's messages to be more 'neurotypical,' effectively automating the exhausting process of masking.
Content moderation AI aggressively removes discussions about self-harm or eating disorders, isolating OCD/Bipolar users looking for peer support and recovery resources.
Friend-recommendation algorithms group neurodivergent people together based on 'shared deficits' inferred from browsing history rather than shared positive interests.
Deepfake technology is used to create ads where trusted neurodivergent influencers appear to endorse 'cures' or dangerous supplements they never agreed to.
Group chat AI summarizers omit 'tangential' points to streamline conversation, consistently silencing the associative thinking style of ND participants.
Digital pills verify medication adherence, but the data is shared with the patient's employer to 'prove fitness for duty,' coercing medication use.
A mental health chatbot uses CBT loops that validate reality, causing distress to a user experiencing schizophrenia who needs grounding, not an argument about logic.
