Now the barriers are automated and there's no staff at the station after 6pm. It's lonely enough in the valleys these days without replacing the last friendly face with a QR code scanner, aye?

There's talk of using drones to patrol the forestry for fly-tipping. I hate the rubbish, mind, it's ych a fi. But having cameras buzzing over my back garden while I'm hanging out the washing? Feels a bit Orwellian for Pontypridd, doesn't it? Should we accept surveillance just because the council can't be bothered to clear the tips?

This gig economy stuff, Uber and that. It's hitting the valleys hard. Lads driving round all hours for pennies, no sick pay, algorithm firing them if they're late. It's worse than the pits in a way—at least the miners had a union. Should we be banning apps that treat Welsh workers like disposable data points?

I tried asking that AI chatbot to write a poem in Welsh, right? It came out speaking gobbledygook, mixing up mutations like a learner on day one. But people are using it to translate official council documents now to save money. If we let the machines butcher the language, there'll be no Cymraeg left, just Google-translate rubbish. We need to stop it, don't we?

My little niece, she's talking to Alexa more than her Mam. But the thing only understands English. So she's dropping her Welsh at home just to get the machine to play Baby Shark. It's colonization by convenience, see? Should tech companies be fined if their smart speakers can't understand a cwtch from a clutch?

S4C wants to put all the old shows on a streaming service, lush. But they're using AI to subtitle it because it's cheaper. The machine doesn't get the jokes or the dialect, does it? It turns 'Now in a minute' into 'Immediately'. It's losing the soul of the culture. Is access worth it if the translation is hanging?

These big American AI models, they've scraped the whole Welsh internet to train their bots. Didn't pay a penny to our authors or poets. Now they're selling it back to us. It's the data equivalent of the drowning of Tryweryn—taking our resources without asking. Shouldn't we own our own language data?

Duolingo is great and that, but everyone's learning 'Standard Welsh'. The dialects from the North and the South are getting flattened out. We're all going to sound like robots from Cardiff. Should we protect the regional dialects in code, or just be happy people are speaking it at all?

Voice banking for people losing their speech, right? It's a brilliant idea. But the NHS tech only offers a generic English voice or a very posh Welsh one. My Dad's a valleys boy; he doesn't want to sound like a newsreader for his last words. Is identity a luxury in healthcare tech?

The Eisteddfod is going hybrid, digital and physical. But the algorithm recommends the pop bands and ignores the traditional choirs because they don't get the clicks. It's skewing the culture towards what goes viral. Should we let an algorithm curate our heritage?

There's a new app for learning Welsh history, but it's funded by the UK government. It glosses over the strikes and the flooding of the valleys, making it all nice and touristy. It's rewriting history with code. Shouldn't we have digital sovereignty over our own stories?

They want to put sensors in the old coal tips to monitor for landslides. Good idea, obviously, after what happened. But the data affects house prices. If the sensor twitches, the value of my terrace house drops to zero. Who sees that data? The insurance companies? It's worrying, mun.

Down Big Pit, they're talking about replacing the ex-miner tour guides with VR headsets. 'Immersive experience' they call it. But you can't replace the stories of a man who actually dug the coal, can you? It's turning our heritage into a video game. Is that respectful to the boys who died down there?

The slate quarries up North, UNESCO site now. Lush. But they want to 3D map the whole thing and sell the digital assets for games. The locals don't see a penny of it. Our landscape made the world's roofs, now it's making someone in London rich again. Who owns the digital rights to a mountain?

Geothermal energy from the flooded mines. Sounds tidy, heating the homes with the warm water. But they need to drill right by the old cemetery. The community is up in arms. Is green tech worth disturbing the ancestors?

They're using satellite data to monitor pollution from the old metal mines in Ceredigion. It shows the rivers are toxic. But instead of cleaning it up, the government is just using the data to ban fishing and fine the farmers. It's data used as a stick, not a broom. Fair play?

A tech company wants to store servers deep underground in the slate caverns. Natural cooling, they say. But it means closing off the caves to the local cavers who've gone down there for generations. Privatising the underground, is it? Just like the coal owners used to do.

Digital archives of the miners' institutes. They're scanning all the old minute books. Great for preservation, but they're putting it behind a paywall! My Grandad wrote those minutes, and now I have to pay a subscription to read them? That's not the socialist way, is it?

Bio-leaching tech—using bacteria to get the last bits of gold out of the Dolgaucau mines. It's 'low impact', they reckon. But if that bacteria gets in the river Teifi, the fish are done for. Are we risking our environment for a few ounces of gold again?

Betsi Cadwaladr health board is in a mess again. They spent millions on a new patient record system that doesn't talk to the English hospitals. My auntie in Chester hospital, the doctors there can't see her notes from Wrexham. It's dangerous, see. Why is digital borders more important than patient safety?

Trying to get a GP appointment in the valleys is impossible. Now they want us to use this 'e-Consult' thing. You type in your symptoms and a computer decides if you're sick enough. I'm not being funny, but how do you explain 'feeling a bit uffar' to an algorithm? It's going to miss things, isn't it?

Mental health support for the farmers, right? They've rolled out a chatbot because there's no therapists in Powys. Telling a suicidal farmer to 'practice mindfulness' via text message? That's insulting. A machine can't offer a cwtch and a cuppa, can it?

Drones delivering prescriptions to the remote cottages in Snowdonia. Sounds futuristic, aye. But what if the drone crashes in the fog? Or gets nicked? Plus, the delivery driver was the only person checking on Mrs Jones all week. We're automating the kindness out of the care.

The NHS app tracks your walking and eating. Gives you 'rewards'. But they're talking about linking it to surgery waiting lists. If you don't hit your step count, you go to the back of the queue for a new hip? That's penalising the poor and the sick, isn't it?

My Nan has dementia, bless her. The council put sensors in her house to track if she's moved. If she stops moving, I get a text. It keeps her safe, but she hates it. Says she feels like a tagged sheep. At what point does safety become a lack of dignity?

Genetic testing for Welsh specific conditions. They want to screen all the babies. But who owns that DNA data? If the insurance companies find out you've got the gene, you're stuffed. We need guarantees before we hand over our blood, right?

Telemedicine is the big thing now. Doctor on a screen. But the broadband in Ceredigion is shocking. The video freezes just as you're showing them your rash. It creates a two-tier system: good health for those with fibre, bad health for those with copper wire. Tidy?

Welsh gov wants to track every single lamb with a digital tag. GPS and all sorts. Cost a fortune, it will. And for what? So some suit in Cardiff can watch dots on a screen? My dog knows where the sheep are. It's solving a problem that doesn't exist and bankrupting the small farms in the process.

Rewilding schemes, right? They've got algorithms deciding which land should be returned to nature for carbon credits. The computer says my top field is 'low yield', so it should be trees. But my family has worked that land for 300 years. An algorithm doesn't know the soil like I do. Is it right to farm by spreadsheet?

Bought a new tractor, John Deere. Lovely bit of kit. But it breaks down and I can't fix it with a spanner. Needs a laptop and a proprietary code. Have to wait a week for a technician from England. I'm losing the harvest waiting for a software update. We need the Right to Repair, don't we?

These carbon trading apps. Big companies buying up Welsh farms to plant trees and offset their pollution. The app makes it easy, click of a button. But it's hollow out the rural communities. No farmers, no school, no pub, just trees and sensors. Is that a green future or a dead one?

Drones for mustering the sheep. Saves the legs, aye. But the sheepdog is part of the family. If we replace the dogs with drones, we lose the training, the bond, the tradition. Some things are worth more than efficiency, surely?

Virtual fencing for the cattle. They wear collars that shock them if they cross a GPS line. No physical fences needed. But if the GPS goes down, the cows are on the A470. And is it cruel to zap a cow because the satellite drifted? I don't trust it, see.

They're gene-editing the Welsh Black cattle to be more methane efficient. Patented genes. If my bull mates with a neighbor's cow, do I owe a corporation royalties for the calf? It's turning nature into intellectual property.

Robotic shearing is coming. 'Safer for the sheep', they say. But shearing is a community event, everyone helps out, bit of food, bit of a laugh. If we automate it, the isolation up here gets even worse. We need neighbors, not just machines, isn't it?

You are a network admin for a security contractor on Nauru. The contract requires strict monitoring of detainee internet usage to prevent 'security breaches,' but you notice the filters are blocking access to Australian legal aid websites and whistleblower portals. Do you whittle down the firewall to allow access to justice, risking your clearance and the company's contract?

An asylum seeker on Manus Island has a smuggled smartphone used to document deteriorating health conditions in the compound. As a systems analyst for the Department of Home Affairs, you've developed a signal triangulation algorithm that could pinpoint the phone's location within meters for confiscation. Do you deploy the code knowing it will silence a whistleblower?

You manage the database for the International Health and Medical Services (IHMS). A new directive requires flagging medical records of detainees approved for 'Medevac' transfer to Australia, specifically looking for inconsistencies that could justify cancellation. Do you run the query that might trap sick people in offshore processing, or corrupt the search results?

Body-worn cameras on guards in immigration detention centres have a 'pre-record' buffer. You are reviewing footage where a guard muted the audio during a physical altercation with a refugee, but the visual buffer clearly shows provocation. The system allows you to permanent-delete 'corrupted' files. Do you preserve the evidence or follow the unofficial culture of protecting the officers?

A facial recognition pilot program is being tested in a detention centre mess hall to 'streamline headcounts.' The system is struggling with darker skin tones, frequently misidentifying individuals and marking them as absent, leading to room raids. Do you halt the trial and report the bias, or tweak the sensitivity thresholds which increases false positives?

You are a drone operator for a private security firm monitoring the perimeter of the Yongah Hill Detention Centre. You spot a detainee attempting self-harm in a blind spot not visible to ground guards. If you zoom in to assess, the footage becomes official property of the ABF and could be used to put the detainee in high-security isolation. Do you record or just radio it in anonymously?

A detainee family on Christmas Island requests a copy of their digital file to fight a deportation order. You know the file contains derogatory metadata notes added by case officers (e.g., 'non-compliant,' 'troublemaker') that aren't legally part of the medical record but will prejudice any judge. Do you scrub the metadata before release or send the raw file?

You manage the 'points system' for a detention centre canteen where good behaviour earns digital credits for phone cards. You notice the algorithm disproportionately penalizes detainees who file formal complaints. Do you patch the code to decouple credits from complaints, knowing management uses this economic leverage to suppress dissent?

Working for Operation Sovereign Borders, you monitor satellite feeds for 'suspect illegal entry vessels.' You spot a wooden boat in distress inside the Indonesian search and rescue zone, but heading for Ashmore Reef. If you log it officially, Australia must respond or turn it back. If you delay the log, it remains Indonesia's problem. What do you do?

You are developing an AI for maritime surveillance that predicts boat arrivals based on weather and moon phases. The model has identified a high-probability window for a departure from Sri Lanka. Sharing this data with local authorities will likely lead to pre-emptive arrests of desperate people; withholding it violates your contract. How do you proceed?

During a 'turnback' operation, Australian Border Force transfers asylum seekers to an orange lifeboat. You are in charge of the lifeboat's GPS tracking module. Your superiors ask you to disable the transponder once it crosses back into international waters to prevent media tracking. Do you comply, knowing it endangers the vessel if it gets lost?

You work in signals intelligence interception. You pick up a distress call from a boat that seems to be sinking. The protocol is to verify the location before dispatching assets, but the signal is weak. You can use a hacked civilian satellite to get a fix, but using that tech is illegal and reveals classified capabilities. Do you break the law to save lives?

A whistleblower wants to leak drone footage proving a boat was in Australian waters when it was pushed back, contradicting the Minister's statement. You are the digital forensics expert asked to authenticate the video timestamp. Confirming it destroys the government's narrative; denying it protects national security interests. What is your verdict?

You are designing a long-range acoustic device (LRAD) for border patrol vessels, intended to broadcast warnings. The specs allow for a frequency setting that causes nausea and disorientation to deter boats from approaching. Do you include this 'non-lethal' deterrent capability in the software firmware?

An automated radar system at Christmas Island keeps flagging legal fishing boats as potential asylum vessels, triggering expensive and aggressive interceptions. You can adjust the algorithm to reduce false positives, but it increases the risk of a refugee boat slipping through undetected. How do you balance efficiency against the 'zero chance' policy?

You are archiving data from a turnback operation. The captain's log contradicts the GPS data regarding the treatment of asylum seekers (pepper spray usage). You are ordered to 'harmonize' the data for the final report to the Senate Estimates committee. Do you alter the digital record?

You are a data analyst for the Department of Home Affairs. A new algorithm is flagging TPV (Temporary Protection Visa) holders for review based on their grocery buying habits (e.g., buying bulk rice/flour suggesting unauthorized shared housing). Do you validate this intrusive model or sabotage the data inputs?

A refugee on a Bridging Visa E is required to report their location via an app every 48 hours. The app is glitching due to a recent update and failing to log check-ins. As the app developer, do you admit the fault publicly, which helps the refugees avoid detention but exposes your company to liability, or blame 'user error'?

You work at Centrelink on the automated compliance system. You notice the system is incorrectly calculating income for SHEV (Safe Haven Enterprise Visa) holders due to their irregular regional work hours, generating false debts. Reporting this pauses the rollout and angers the Minister. Do you whistleblow or let the 'computer say no'?

An asylum seeker's 'Code of Behaviour' prohibits 'anti-social' online activity. You are tasked with training a bot to scrape Facebook comments of visa holders for keywords like 'protest' or 'union.' Do you narrow the scope to actual threats of violence, or broaden it to include political dissent as requested by the client?

A TPV holder is working cash-in-hand to survive because their visa conditions restrict work rights. You are integrating ATO (Tax Office) data with Immigration databases. Do you enable the specific API hook that matches bank deposit patterns to visa holders, effectively creating a deportation trap?

You assist with the 'Fast Track' assessment process. The AI translation tool used for applicant interviews is struggling with the Hazaragi dialect, frequently mistranslating crucial details about persecution. Continuing to use it speeds up the backlog; stopping for human translators causes years of delay. What do you recommend?

A digital ID system is being proposed for refugees to access services, replacing paper cards. The system requires a central database that foreign governments (including the ones they fled) could theoretically hack or request access to via Interpol. Do you architect the system with a backdoor for law enforcement?

You are an admin for the ImmiAccount portal. A server migration has caused some asylum applications to vanish. You can restore them from a backup, but the timestamps will reset to today, potentially making the applicants ineligible due to missed deadlines. Do you manually edit the timestamps to the correct past date, which is technically forgery?

You are designing an HR screening tool for a large Australian retail chain. The algorithm automatically rejects CVs with unexplained gaps of over 3 years. This filters out almost all refugees who were in offshore detention. Do you create a specific 'exemption' flag for refugees, risking claims of 'reverse discrimination,' or leave the bias in?

A newly settled refugee from Afghanistan has no paper documents for their engineering degree. You are working on a blockchain credentialing pilot. The university in Kabul has been taken over by the Taliban and won't verify. Do you accept a 'statutory declaration' plus a skills test as a digital equivalent, or strictly require source verification?

You run a rental application platform. Landlords are asking for a feature to filter out applicants who receive Centrelink payments or have 'uncertain visa status.' Implementing this increases your market share with agents but effectively makes refugees homeless. Do you build the filter?

A gig-economy delivery app is the only source of income for many refugees. The app's facial recognition security check often fails for dark-skinned users or those with facial scarring (common in torture survivors), locking them out of work. Do you relax the security threshold, increasing fraud risk, or keep it strict?

You are a MyGov UX designer. The current interface is impossible for someone with low English literacy and no digital history (e.g., post-Nauru). Management wants to push a 'digital-first' strategy that removes phone support. Do you fight for a simplified, multi-lingual 'lite' version even if it blows the budget?

A refugee support agency wants to use a predictive model to decide where to settle new arrivals (e.g., regional towns vs cities). The model suggests sending them to towns with cheap housing but high racism/unemployment. Do you optimize the algorithm for 'economic cost' or 'social integration'?

You work for a bank implementing 'Know Your Customer' (KYC) automation. Refugees on bridging visas often lack the standard 100 points of ID. Do you create a manual override workflow for them, which costs the bank money and time, or let the system auto-reject their account applications?

A language learning app uses voice data to grade pronunciation. It consistently marks the accents of Sudanese refugees as 'incorrect,' impeding their certification for work readiness. Do you retrain the AI with a more diverse dataset, which takes months, or release the product now to meet the government grant deadline?

A refugee is trying to prove a relationship with his wife in Iran for a spousal visa. They have no marriage certificate, only years of WhatsApp logs. You are the digital forensics officer. The logs contain anti-regime sentiments that could endanger her if the report is leaked or shared with Iranian authorities. Do you redact the political content, risking the evidence looking 'edited' and rejected?

You work for a remittance app. Sanctions on countries like Syria or Afghanistan make transferring money legally difficult. You can route the transactions through a third-country 'grey' channel to help refugees feed their families, but it violates Australian financial tracking laws. Do you patch the route?

The Department of Home Affairs demands DNA testing for family reunification. You manage the genetic database. A request comes in to cross-reference this refugee DNA data with a crime scene cold case database. The consent forms signed by the refugees were for 'visa purposes only.' Do you allow the cross-match?

A refugee in Sydney wants to use VR technology to 'visit' his dying mother in a strictly controlled conflict zone. You can set up the connection, but it requires using a VPN and software that is banned in the mother's country. If caught, she faces arrest. Do you facilitate the virtual goodbye?

You are reviewing 'proof of relationship' social media scrapes. You find a photo of the applicant with a different partner from 10 years ago. It’s likely irrelevant, but could be used by a case officer to claim the current marriage is a sham. Do you include this 'discovery' in your final report?

An asylum seeker has lost contact with their child during a boat crossing. You have access to a facial recognition database of unaccompanied minors in Indonesian shelters. Running the parent's photo against the database violates international data sharing protocols. Do you run the search anyway?

You are building a secure communication tool for refugees to talk to lawyers. The Australian government passes the 'Assistance and Access Bill' requiring a backdoor for encryption. Do you build the backdoor, compromising the safety of families back home who discuss persecution, or refuse and face jail time?

A Somali refugee wants to livestream a family wedding happening in Mogadishu to the community hall in Melbourne. The only available internet link is monitored by a local militia who demands a 'digital tax' (crypto payment) to keep the connection open. Do you help facilitate this payment (funding a militia) to allow the family connection?

Look mate, the government reckons this new satellite internet is the ducks nuts for the bush, but it costs an arm and a leg. My neighbour's kids can't do their schoolwork because they can't afford the connection fees. Is it fair dinkum to make education reliant on tech that half the station owners can't access?

I bought this massive yank tank tractor, top of the line, right? But the software's locked down tighter than a fish's backside. If a sensor busts in the middle of harvest, I can't fix it with a spanner; I gotta fly a bloke out from Sydney. I own the metal, but do I own the machine if I can't repair it?

These ag-tech mobs are putting sensors all over my paddocks to monitor soil moisture. Helpful, yeah, but then they aggregate that data and sell the yield predictions to the futures market before I've even harvested. Seems a bit rich that they're making cash off my dirt while I'm taking all the risk.

We've got drones checking the fences now, saves riding the boundary for days. But the footage captures the neighbour's missus sunbaking in her backyard. The law says the airspace is clear, but out here, privacy is sacred. Do I delete the footage or keep it for 'security'?

Telehealth is great for a chat, but this AI diagnostic tool reckoned my skin cancer was 'benign' because it was trained on city folk who don't spend 12 hours a day in the sun. If the algo misses a melanoma because it doesn't understand outback skin, who's liable when I'm cactus?

The water authority put smart meters on the river pumps to stop blokes pinching water. Fair enough. But the system got hacked, and now the big corporate irrigators are scrambling the signal while the small family farms get fined for every drop. How's that a level playing field?

Emergency beacons are essential out past the black stump. Now they're pushing these app-based ones that rely on a subscription. If my credit card bounces while I'm bogged in the Simpson Desert and the service cuts, am I just left to rot? Safety shouldn't be a subscription service.

They're rolling out autonomous road trains to haul cattle. Safer, they say. But that's half the town's jobs gone. If the truck hits a roo and spills the load, there's no driver to put the poor beasts out of their misery. Just a computer sending an error code to Perth.

Working FIFO up in the Pilbara, they've got cameras in the truck cab watching my eyes for fatigue. Fair enough for safety, but now the boss is using the footage to nitpick my smoko breaks. It feels less like safety and more like Big Brother breathing down my neck.

The company wants us to wear these smart wristbands at the donga (camp) to track our sleep and 'readiness for work'. Mate, what I do in my off hours is my business. If I have a restless night, does the algo decide I don't get a shift—and don't get paid—the next day?

We're automating the drill rigs. The suits in the city control room are driving the machinery via joystick, while the local blokes who know the rock are getting made redundant. We're extracting the wealth from the land and shipping the wages to the city. Is that right for the local community?

The environmental sensors around the mine site are automated now. The data goes straight to the company server, not the EPA. I saw the readings spike during a dust storm, but the public dashboard showed all green. Do I blow the whistle and lose my job, or trust the 'glitch' will be fixed?

They're using AI to screen job applicants for the mines now. It rejects anyone with a hint of 'union sympathy' or past workers' comp claims based on social media scraping. It's blacklisting good workers before they even get a foot in the door.

Standard procedure is to track all company vehicles with GPS. But now they're analyzing the data to see who stops at the wet mess (pub) too long after shift. It's legal, but it's treating grown men like school kids. Breaks the trust in the crew, doesn't it?

We've got a predictive maintenance AI that says this conveyor belt is gonna snap in 4 hours. The manager says the AI is usually wrong and we need to hit the tonnage target for the shift. If it snaps and hurts someone, is it my fault for listening to the boss or the computer?

Post-COVID, they kept the contact tracing badges active underground. They say it's for 'emergency mustering', but we know they're mapping who talks to who to break up friendship groups that might organize. It's union-busting disguised as safety tech.

Some researchers mapped the Songlines using GIS for preservation. Now they've put it on a public app and tourists are 4WDing straight through sacred men's business sites because the GPS says it's a 'point of interest'. How do we digitize culture without losing control of it?

The government is digitizing all the old mission records. Auntie's trauma from the Stolen Generations is in those files. She doesn't want it searchable on the net for any curious bugger to read. Who owns that data? The state that wrote it, or the Mob it was written about?

Tech giants are coming into communities recording Elders speaking language to train AI models. They say it's 'preservation', but then they copyright the model. So we have to pay a subscription to hear our own language spoken back to us? That's just colonialism with code.

The cops are using predictive policing AI in town. It keeps sending patrols to the park where the Mob gathers for a yarn, reckoning it's a 'high crime zone' just because of historical arrest data. It's creating a feedback loop of harassment. How's that fair?

To buy groceries at the community store, they've installed a facial recognition system linked to the BasicsCard. You don't scan, you don't eat. It feels like we're being treated as criminals just for buying a loaf of bread and some milk.

We want to use drones to monitor Country for illegal dumping and fires. But the regulations say we need a certified pilot from the city. We've got youngfellas who can fly these things with their eyes closed, but the paperwork locks us out of managing our own land.

Genomic research wants DNA from Indigenous Australians to 'close the gap' in health outcomes. But last time, they used the blood samples for something else entirely without asking. If we give data to the cloud, how do we ensure Indigenous Data Sovereignty is respected?

Artists in the community are seeing their styles copied by generative AI. It spits out 'Aboriginal-style' dot paintings in seconds. It's stealing the spirit of the art and undercutting the livelihood of real artists. Is it legal? Maybe. Is it moral? No way.

The government is pushing this cashless gaming card for the pokies. Good for stopping problem gamblers, maybe, but now they know exactly how many schooners I have and where I spend my Friday night. It's a slippery slope to tracking every cent I spend.

My rental in Melbourne just installed smart locks. The landlord wants a face scan to issue the key. I told him to rack off, I want a physical key, but he reckons it's 'condition of entry'. Since when did renting a flat mean giving up my biometric data?

Transport for NSW tracks my Opal card. They know I go from Parramatta to the CBD every day at 8am. Now they're selling 'aggregated' movement data to developers. They say it's anonymous, but it wouldn't take a genius to figure out it's me.

Robodebt was a disaster, but they're still trying to use algorithms to cross-match my tax and welfare. Computer says I owe 'em two grand. I don't, but the burden of proof is on me to prove the machine is wrong. It's guilty until proven innocent by algorithm.

These e-scooters in Brisbane are geofenced. If I ride into a 'slow zone', the thing slams on the brakes automatically. It's dangerous if you're in traffic. Who's responsible if the GPS drifts and creates an accident—me or the software dev?

Smart electricity meters allow the power company to throttle my air con during a heatwave to 'save the grid'. I pay the bill, shouldn't I decide how cool my house is? Especially when the vulnerable elderly are the ones suffering the most.

The cops want access to everyone's Ring doorbell footage to solve crimes. It sounds good for catching thieves, but suddenly my front porch is part of a suburb-wide surveillance network. I didn't sign up to be a snitch for the police state.

Workplace monitoring software tracks my keystrokes and mouse movement while I'm working from home. If I go put the kettle on, my 'productivity score' drops. We used to judge work by output, now we're judging it by how much we act like robots.

We're using AI to predict bushfire paths. The model says my property is in the 'red zone' for next season, so the insurance company tripled my premium. I've cleared the scrub and done the right thing, but the algo says I'm uninsurable. Computer says burn.

Scientists are using drones to monitor the Great Barrier Reef. The data shows severe bleaching in a popular tourist spot. The tour operators want the data suppressed so the tourists don't stop coming. Do we protect the economy or tell the truth about the environment?

They've released these gene-drive modified mosquitoes to stop Dengue up north. Brilliant science, but if it mutates or jumps species, we can't exactly recall 'em. We're playing god with the ecosystem and hoping she'll be right.

Automated feral cat traps use AI to identify the target. If it sees a cat, it sprays poison. If it sees a wallaby, it leaves it. But what if the lens is dirty or the AI glitches and it sprays a dingo or a pet dog? Automating death in the bush is risky business.

Shark-spotting drones are patrolling the beaches. Great for safety, but they're also filming everyone in their swimmers. The footage is supposed to be deleted, but who's checking? It's a bit creepy having a camera hovering over you while you're having a dip.

We found a new grove of Wollemi Pines, proper rare stuff. I took a photo, but forgot to scrub the GPS metadata. Now I'm worried some collector will find the coordinates online and raid the site. Should social media platforms auto-scrub location data for endangered species?

Commercial fishing boats are turning off their AIS (tracking) systems to sneak into protected marine parks at night. We can see them on satellite radar, but without the transponder ID, we can't prosecute. We need tech that forces them to stay visible, but they claim 'privacy' for their fishing spots.

Tagging koalas with radio collars provides great data, but the new collars are bulky and seem to stress the poor little buggers out. Is the data we get worth the misery we cause the animal? Sometimes I reckon we should just leave 'em be.

The Council are after putting up these smart cameras at the entrance to the halting site, saying it's for 'fly-tipping prevention', but the lads reckon it's facial recognition tracking who's coming and going. It's capturing the childer playing and all. Do we smash the camera to protect our privacy, or try to lodge a GDPR complaint that'll take three years to process while they watch us every day?

I'm trying to get insurance for the van, but the algorithm sees the halting site address and the quote goes through the roof, pure extortion. It's redlining, plain and simple. Do I use my settled cousin's address in town to get a fair price, even if it invalidates the policy, or accept that the computer is programmed to discriminate against Travellers?

There's a genetic research crowd from the university wanting DNA samples from the community to study 'Traveller-specific heritage'. They promise it's for medical history, but we've been burned before with data being used to claim we're 'different' in a bad way. Do we participate to maybe cure conditions in the family, or block them from the site to stop them harvesting our data?

The new Eircode system is a disaster for us. The bay doesn't have a fixed code, so I can't register for the social welfare online or get a parcel delivered. I'm invisible to the system. Do I squat digitally on a nearby empty house's Eircode, or campaign for a 'nomadic digital ID' that the government keeps ignoring?

Young lads are posting videos on TikTok explaining Pavee culture, but the comments are absolutely vile, pure hate speech. The platform's AI isn't catching the slang insults used against us. Do we report it and risk the algorithm shadowbanning our own educational videos, or just disable comments and silence the dialogue?

The school gave the childer iPads for homework, which is grand, but there's no WiFi in the trailer and the site has no broadband infrastructure. The school software tracks 'engagement' and marks them down for not logging in. Do we hack the nearby industrial estate's WiFi to get the homework done, or let the kids fail because the infrastructure ignores us?

A digital archive is digitizing old photos of Travellers from the 60s, but they're tagging people with incorrect settled names and descriptions that are fairly insulting. They say 'open access' is key. Do we demand they take the archive down until a Traveller approves every tag, erasing history in the meantime, or let the wrong history stand?

The Gardaí are using a predictive policing map that lights up our site like a Christmas tree just because of historical arrest data, not current crime. It means a squad car is parked outside the gate 24/7. Do we flood the system with noise—false reports in posh areas—to skew their algorithm back to neutral?

The management at the Direct Provision centre have installed a fingerprint scanner for the canteen. No scan, no dinner. They say it's for 'efficiency', but it feels like prison tech. Do we boycott the food hall and go hungry to protest the biometrics, or submit our data just to get a hot meal?

The WiFi in the centre is shocking slow and blocks WhatsApp calls, which is the only way I can talk to my mother back home. The management says it's to 'preserve bandwidth'. Do I set up a mesh network with a smuggled 5G router for the whole floor, risking eviction, or stay isolated?

I've been in the system five years now. The Department of Justice has terabytes of data on my movements, my health, my kids. If I finally get my papers, they keep that data 'just in case'. Do I have the right to demand a 'digital clean slate' upon citizenship, or does my time in the centre mark me forever in the database?

We're three families in one room, and the kids are doing online schooling. There's no privacy; the camera sees everything, the drying clothes, the stress. The other kids in the Zoom call are making fun of the background. Do I force the child to keep the camera off and get marked absent, or expose our living conditions to the class?

A local 'concerned residents' group is flying a drone over the centre to 'check for overcrowding'. It's filming us in the yard. The Guards say it's a civil matter. Do we use a signal jammer to drop the drone, risking legal trouble, or let them livestream our limbo?

I'm not allowed to work, but I can rent a Deliveroo account from a lad in town. It's the only way to get cash for the kids. The app's facial recognition check is coming up. Do I ask the account owner to verify it (identity fraud), or starve on the €38.80 weekly allowance?

The centre manager is sharing 'incident reports' (like missing a curfew by 5 minutes) with the International Protection Office. An algorithm uses this to assess 'good character' for the application. Do I hack the logbook to delete these minor infractions, or trust a system that seems designed to fail me?

The new EU border system requires a pre-check app. My brother is trying to get here. The app tracks location and contacts. If I download it to help him, I link my device (and my precarious status) to his illegal crossing attempt. Do I risk my own asylum claim to help him navigate the digital border?

The HSE website's auto-translate is talking absolute shite, putting 'pole' instead of 'Polish person', and the elderly in the community can't book their scans. The government says a proper translation is 'too expensive'. Do we build a community scraper to overlay correct Polish, risking copyright strikes, or let the old ones suffer?

I'm working construction, and the foreman is using an app to track our location even when we're off the clock, saying it's for 'insurance'. Most of the lads are Polish and afraid to speak up. Do we coordinate a mass data-poisoning event (leaving phones on a bus), or is that risking our jobs?

We're trying to organize a union for Polish care workers, but Facebook is suppressing the posts because the algorithm thinks the mix of Polish and English is 'spam' or 'disinformation'. Do we switch to encrypted Telegram channels, losing the visibility to the wider Irish public, or fight the algorithm?

The Irish banks are a nightmare to deal with, asking for utility bills I don't have in my name. Everyone is using Revolut, but now Revolut is freezing accounts of Polish nationals for 'security checks' more than Irish locals. Do we create a community credit union on the blockchain, or is that just asking for a Revenue audit?

The secondary school uses an algorithm to stream students. It consistently puts Polish kids in lower English streams despite them being fluent, just based on their surname. Do I tell my daughter to change her name on the form to something 'more Irish' to get into Higher Level, or fight the school board?

The government is offering a 'digital repatriation' grant to help us move back to Poland, linking our Irish tax data to Polish systems. It feels like they're trying to automate us out of the country. Do we consent to the data transfer to get the grant, or refuse and stay in a housing market that's pushing us out?

A major Irish news site uses an AI to generate headlines, and it always frames Eastern European crime stories with sensationalist language compared to locals. It's stirring up anti-immigrant sentiment. Do we launch a bot attack on their comment section to highlight the bias, or write a letter they'll ignore?

The online voter registration for local elections is grand if you have an Irish passport, but a total labyrinth for EU citizens, asking for forms that don't exist. It feels like digital voter suppression. Do I build a tool to auto-fill these forms for the community, risking legal action for 'interfering with elections'?

The facial recognition gates at Dublin Airport never work for me or the lads; it struggles with darker skin tones. We always get pulled aside for 'manual processing' while the white folks breeze through. Do we start a campaign to jam the queues by refusing to use the e-gates, or accept the 'glitch' as part of life here?

I'm applying for rentals in Dublin. If I use my full Nigerian name on Daft.ie, I get zero replies. If I use 'Mo' and no photo, I get viewings. The platforms claim they're neutral. Do I build a browser extension that anonymizes names for landlords until the viewing, or is that 'deceiving' the property owner?

I'm creating content about being Black and Irish, growing up in Balbriggan. TikTok's algorithm suppresses my videos if I mention 'racism', but boosts them if I just do dances. Do I censor my own experience to get the views, or stay authentic and invisible?

The Garda Youth Diversion Programme uses a risk assessment tool. It seems to flag Black Irish teenagers as 'high risk' for gang activity based on postcode and peer groups, not actual crimes. Do we tell the young lads to leave their phones at home so they aren't digitally mapped into a gang they aren't part of?

I drive a taxi using an app. I've noticed I get fewer pickups in certain affluent areas when my profile photo is visible. The algorithm then downgrades me for 'low acceptance' when I don't get jobs. Do I use a cartoon avatar (against terms of service) to feed my family, or fight the black box?

Sending money back to Lagos via Western Union is a rip-off. We want to use crypto, but the Irish banks are flagging any crypto transaction from Nigerian-named accounts as 'potential money laundering'. Do we move to a decentralized peer-to-peer system that's technically unregulated, or let the banks take their 15% cut?

The AI diagnostic tool used in the maternity hospital was trained on white datasets. It misses signs of complications in black women's skin (like jaundice or cyanosis). Do I demand a manual check every time, being labelled a 'difficult patient', or trust the machine that might kill me?

I have a thick Dublin accent, but voice assistants (Siri/Alexa) struggle because I don't sound like their training data for 'Irish' or 'Nigerian'. It's a small thing, but it locks me out of voice banking. Do I put on a fake 'posh' voice to bank, or demand they train the model on the new Ireland?

Living in Derry, working in Donegal. My phone is constantly switching networks. The UK provider wants to charge roaming now post-Brexit, and the data tells them I'm 'abroad' half the day. Do I run a VPN to pretend I'm always in the North to save the bill, or is that fraud against the telecom giant?

There's a project to digitize old RUC interrogation tapes using AI to transcribe them. It might reveal truths about the Troubles, but it also exposes informants who were promised anonymity. If this data leaks, people will be shot. Do we support the 'truth recovery' or hack the project to delete the names?

A new 'shared housing' algorithm allocates social housing to try and mix communities. But it's putting Protestant families in deep Republican areas and vice versa without checking the 'safety' on the ground. The computer says it's efficient; the locals say it's dangerous. Do we sabotage the data to keep the peace lines intact?

After the PSNI data breach, we know they have a list of all staff. Now dissident groups are using facial recognition on public social media to match names to faces. Do I scrub my entire digital existence and disconnect from my family online, or demand the police give us new identities?

The Stormont portal for benefits doesn't accept Irish characters (fadas) in names, returning 'Invalid Entry'. My legal name is in Irish. Do I anglicize my name to get my heating allowance, betraying my identity, or freeze while fighting for a software patch?

They're putting 'smart gates' on the Peace Walls that open and close automatically based on 'threat levels' detected by AI listening for gunshots or crowds. If the AI hallucinates a riot, it locks us in. Do we trust the automated peace, or demand a human with a key?

The Census online form forces a binary choice in some sections or defaults to 'Northern Irish' if you skip. It's messing with the demographics that determine the border poll future. Do we organize a campaign to fill the form incorrectly to break their data, or accept the digital compromise?

There's still cameras pointing at the Catholic areas that date back years, now upgraded with HD. They say it's for 'traffic', but it points at the club. The lads want to use lasers to blind the sensors. Is that vandalism, or legitimate defense against a surveillance state that never really left?

I'm working down in the Silicon Docks for one of the big lads, writing the algorithm that keeps people scrolling on the timeline. The engagement metrics are through the roof, fair play to us, but I'm after seeing my young niece at Sunday dinner glued to the screen, totally anxious, ignoring the family. It's my code doing that to her. Do I keep taking the massive salary to pay the rent in D4, or do I flag that we're actively breaking people's brains for ad revenue?

Your man from California flies in and tells us we need to train the AI on Irish language data to be inclusive. Grand idea, except he wants us to scrape everything from TG4 and the Gaeltacht archives without asking permission or paying a cent to the creators. It feels like digital colonialism, so it does. Do I build the scraper or tell him where to shove his 'inclusivity'?

The housing crisis in Dublin is fierce, and here I am coding a platform that helps landlords optimize short-term lets for tourists rather than long-term tenants. My own mates are emigrating because they can't find a place to live, and I'm basically automating their eviction. Is it enough to say 'it's just a tool', or am I part of the problem?

We're handling content moderation for the whole EU right here in Sandyford. The stuff I'm seeing would turn your stomach—absolute filth. We're under strict NDAs not to talk about it, but the mental health support is a joke—an app and a cup of tea. If I leak the working conditions to the papers, I'll be sued into oblivion, but if I stay quiet, the burnout is going to kill someone.

Sure look, the company is paying barely any tax here thanks to the 'Double Irish' legacy setups and IP shifting. I'm proud of the work we do, but when I walk past the homeless tents on the canal to get to our shiny glass office with free food, the guilt is eating me alive. Should I push for an internal CSR initiative, or is that just putting lipstick on a pig?

My team is developing facial recognition for 'security', but we know well it's going to be sold to regimes that aren't exactly democratic. The boss says, 'If we don't build it in Dublin, they'll build it in Shenzhen.' Is that a valid excuse to write code that could lock up protestors, or am I just washing my hands of it?

We're launching a new feature that tracks user location 'to improve service', but I know for a fact the data is being packaged and sold to insurers. It's technically legal under the Terms of Service nobody reads, but it feels fierce shady. Do I whistleblow to the Data Protection Commission and risk my career in this town?

The 'culture' in the office is all beanbags and free beer, but they're cracking down on anyone trying to unionize. They're monitoring our internal Slack channels for keywords like 'union' or 'representation'. I'm the admin with access to the logs. Do I warn the organizers they're being watched, or do I protect my own job and say nothing?

The National Broadband Plan has been 'coming soon' for donkey's years. I've a chance to set up a community mesh network using some grey-market gear to get the valley connected so the kids can do their homework. It's not strictly legal by ComReg standards, but the government has left us rotting. Do I break the law to get the village online?

I'm a farmer in Tipp, and these new automated tractors are grand, but John Deere locks the software so I can't fix it myself with a spanner anymore. I have to pay a technician a fortune to come out and press a button. Someone offered me a cracked firmware that lets me repair my own gear. Is it ethical to pirate the software of the tractor I own, just to keep the farm running?

The local pub is dying on its feet because everyone's at home on Netflix or scrolling TikTok. I'm developing an app to help rural pubs market themselves, but it relies on gamifying drinking—points for pints, essentially. Am I saving the community hub by encouraging alcoholism, or is the pub culture dead anyway?

My elderly mother is alone out in Connemara. I want to install a full sensor suite—cameras, motion detectors, the works—so I can watch her from Dublin. She says she hates the idea of being spied on, but she's had a fall before. Do I override her dignity for her safety, or leave her be and risk finding her too late?

A big tech crowd wants to test their delivery drones in our area because the airspace is empty. It'll bring a few jobs to the local hub, but the noise is driving the sheep mad and annoying the locals who moved here for the quiet. Do we take the foreign investment and lose the peace, or tell them to buzz off?

We're using AI to analyze soil samples to reduce fertilizer use, which is great for the environment. But the data goes straight to a multinational that's using it to buy up the most productive land, pushing out small family farms. I'm helping the environment but killing the community. What's the right move?

The GAA club wants to use a new app for managing the underage teams, but it demands a rake of data on the kids—location, health info, parents' details. I'm the only one on the committee who understands GDPR and sees the risk, but if I block it, I'm the eejit stopping the club from modernizing. Do I hold the line?

Tourism is the only thing keeping the town afloat, and Airbnb is driving it. But now, no local can afford to rent a house. I've built a bot that helps locals snatch up long-term rentals the second they go online, giving them an unfair advantage over the tourists. Is it fair to rig the market to save the village?

Living right on the border near Newry, and the police want to put up 'Smart Border' cameras that track every car crossing over. They say it's for catching smugglers, but given the history of this place, people are fierce paranoid about surveillance. I've been asked to consult on the tech. Do I help make it efficient, or refuse and let them build a botched system that might be worse?

Post-Brexit, the data sharing between the NHS in the North and the HSE in the South is a legal minefield. I have a patient who crosses the border daily. Do I share their medical file informally via encrypted email to ensure they get treatment, breaking the data laws, or stick to the protocol and risk their health?

I'm moderating a local community forum for a border town. The algorithms are flagging terms that are part of our daily vernacular as 'hate speech' because they don't understand the context, while missing actual sectarian dog-whistles. Do I train the AI on the slang, potentially teaching it how to be a better bigot, or keep doing it manually and drowning in the toxicity?

A company wants to map the 'Peace Walls' in Belfast for a mixed-reality history tour app. It sounds grand, educational. But locals are worried it'll turn their trauma into a theme park for tourists and maybe even identify homes of people who want to stay anonymous. Is some history better left un-digitized?

With the different regulations now, I can route our company's user data through a server in Belfast to bypass some strict Dublin EU rules, or vice versa. It's a legal grey area—the 'digital border' is porous. It saves the company millions. Am I a cute hoor for spotting the loophole, or undermining the law?

The PSNI (Police Service of Northern Ireland) had that massive data breach where officers' names were leaked. I run a cybersecurity firm and I've found a copy of the list on the dark web. Do I buy it to secure it and hand it over, knowing I'm funding the criminals, or leave it out there where paramilitaries might find it?

We're building a genealogy app, and in the border counties, DNA tests are bringing up secrets about who's related to who from the Troubles era. It's causing unmerciful rows and distress. Should we suppress matches that suggest 'non-paternal events' in this specific region to keep the peace, or is the truth the truth?

Drones are being used to monitor illegal dumping and diesel smuggling along the border. The locals are shooting them down, saying it's spy gear. I supply the drones. Do I arm them with better tracking and altitude capabilities to outsmart the locals, or accept that in border country, surveillance is an act of aggression?

We're building another massive data center on the outskirts of Dublin. The grid is creaking; we've been told there might be brownouts this winter for regular houses, but our contract guarantees us power 24/7. Is it right to keep the servers cool for TikTok videos while Mrs. Murphy down the road might lose her heating?

A tech giant wants to build a data center in a rural area, promising construction jobs. But once it's built, it'll employ about ten people and consume the water of a medium-sized town. The council is broke and needs the rates (taxes). Do I vote to approve it for the short-term cash, knowing it's a long-term parasite?

I manage the cooling systems. We could run them hotter to save energy—the servers can take it—but it increases the risk of a crash by 0.5%. Management says '100% uptime' is the god we worship. Do I secretly adjust the setpoints to save megawatts of power, hoping nobody notices?

We're offsetting our carbon emissions by planting trees, but not in Ireland—we're buying cheap credits in South America. Meanwhile, our diesel generators in Clondalkin are running full tilt during peak hours. It's greenwashing, pure and simple. Do I sign off on the sustainability report?

There's a proposal to hook the data center's waste heat into a district heating system for a new housing estate. Sounds brilliant, but it locks those houses into dependency on the tech company. If the company leaves or upgrades the tech, the heating goes. Is it a symbiotic relationship or a hostage situation?

The planning permission requires us to protect the local biodiversity. There's a badger sett right where the backup generator needs to go. My boss says, 'Sure, they're nocturnal, move them at night and nobody will know.' Do I report the violation and delay a billion-euro project, or let the badgers take one for the digital economy?

We're storing data for countries with terrible human rights records because Ireland is considered a 'safe haven'. The servers are physically here, protected by Irish law, but the data is being used to oppress people abroad. Are we complicit by providing the digital vault?

Local residents are protesting the noise of the fans. We can build sound baffles, but they're expensive and reduce efficiency. The legal limit allows the noise, but it's wrecking the neighbours' sleep. Do strictly follow the law, or do the decent thing and spend the money to be a good neighbour?

Sure look, the Data Protection Commission (DPC) is swamped. I'm working there, and I have a file on a massive breach by a US tech giant that affects millions. But I've been told to prioritize 'amicable resolution' because the government is terrified of the multinationals pulling out of Dublin. Do I bury the file or leak it to Max Schrems?

I'm a consultant advising small Irish businesses. A local GAA club keeps a spreadsheet of members' details on an unsecured laptop. Strictly speaking, I should report them or force them to buy expensive software they can't afford. Do I turn a blind eye because 'it's only the lads', or enforce the law?

The 'One Stop Shop' mechanism means Ireland regulates for the whole EU. Other European regulators are raging at us, saying we're too soft. I'm in a meeting where we're discussing a fine that's pocket change to the company. If I speak up and say it's too low, I'm 'anti-business'. If I don't, I'm failing 400 million Europeans. What's the craic?

We're designing a 'consent cookie' banner. The client wants the 'Reject All' button to be grey and hidden in a submenu, while 'Accept All' is bright green. It's technically compliant but manipulative—'dark patterns', they call it. Do I design it to trick my own granny, or insist on a fair interface?

A US company is threatening to move 500 jobs to Switzerland if the DPC enforces a strict interpretation of data transfer rules. I'm a civil servant; my job is to protect Irish interests. Is protecting Irish jobs more important than the abstract privacy rights of a German citizen?

I have access to the 'Right to be Forgotten' requests. A local politician wants links to an old scandal removed. It's in the public interest, but he's arguing it's 'outdated and irrelevant'. If I approve it, I'm helping him sanitize his past before an election. If I refuse, he'll make my life hell. What do I do?

We're implementing age verification for an Irish social media site to protect kids. But to do it, we need users to upload passports or IDs, creating a massive honeypot of identity data. We're trading privacy for safety. Is it worth the risk of that database getting hacked?

The EU is demanding we fine a company billions. The fines go to the Irish exchequer, which sounds grand, but it makes us look like we're profiteering from enforcement. The company is offering a settlement that includes building a new park and community centre in Dublin 4. Do we take the bribe—sorry, the 'settlement'—or the fine?

We've got a tech giant from California wantin' to scrape our entire corpus of Gaelic literature to train their LLM. They say it'll save the language by makin' it digital, but they're no payin' a penny to the writers or the families of the bards who kept the tongue alive during the hard times. Is it cultural preservation or just colonial extraction all over again?

The new predictive text on the bairns' phones keeps correctin' perfectly good Gaelic grammar into English sentence structures. It's subtle, but it's changin' how the young ones form their thoughts. Should we be banin' these 'smart' keyboards in the Gaelic Medium schools to stop the anglicisation of the syntax?

An AI voice synthesiser has been trained on the recordings of a famous Lewis seanchaidh (storyteller) who passed away years ago. His family is upset that his voice is readin' news bulletins and weather reports he never spoke. Does the community own the voice of the tradition, or does the data belong to the archives that digitised it?

Duolingo is great for the tourists, but the elders are sayin' it's teachin' a 'standardised' Gaelic that ignores the rich dialects of Islay or Uist. If we let an algorithm decide what 'correct' Gaelic is, are we flattenin' our heritage just to make it fit into a database?

We have a chance to put Gaelic into a massive voice recognition system, but it struggles with the older speakers who have the deepest vocabulary. If the system only learns from the young ones with lighter accents, are we codin' ageism right into the revival efforts?

A chatbot has been released to help learners practice Gaelic, but it hallucinates idioms that don't exist. Now we have learners comin' to the Gaidhealtachd usin' phrases that make no sense, insistin' the computer is right. How do we police the purity of the language against a machine that sounds so confident?

Google Translate is finally addin' better Gaelic support, but it's crowdsourcin' corrections from anyone on the internet. We're seein' trolls deliberately feedin' it wrong translations. Do we need a 'digital council of elders' to gatekeep the data, or is that against the open spirit of the web?

There's a debate about 'Gaelic-ish' AI art—generatin' Celtic knotwork and patterns that look Scottish but have no actual meanin' or history. Is it harmless fun, or is it dilutin' our visual language with meaningless algorithmic noise?

The Council wants to use AI tutoring systems for Higher Gaelic because we can't find enough qualified teachers for the remote schools in the Highlands. Is it fair to the rural pupils to be taught by a machine while the Inverness kids get real teachers?

In the Gaelic Medium Units, the tablets provided by the government have operating systems that are only in English. The interface itself is teachin' the kids that English is the language of technology and Gaelic is just for history. Should we refuse the tech until it speaks our tongue?

We're seein' pupils usin' AI to write their Gaelic essays. The teachers canna always tell. If a lad uses ChatGPT to write a poem for the Mòd (Gaelic festival), and wins, has he cheated, or is he just usin' the tools of his time? What does this do to the oral tradition?

e-Sgoil (e-school) has been a lifeline, beam in' lessons to the islands. But now the council suggests closin' the physical village school entirely and goin' full remote to save cash. Is a school just a content delivery system, or is the buildin' the heart of the community?

There's new software for screenin' dyslexia, but it's calibrated on English phonics. It's flaggin' half our Gaelic Medium kids as havin' learnin' difficulties just because the sounds don't match the English model. Is it ethical to use these diagnostic tools on GME pupils?

A developer wants to gamify Gaelic history for the classroom, turnin' the Jacobite risings into an RPG. Some parents worry it trivialises the slaughter and turns our ancestors' struggle into 'points' and 'levels'. Where's the line between engagement and disrespect?

Digital textbooks are cheaper, but they can be updated instantly. We're worried a government in Edinburgh might quietly sanitise the history of the Clearances in the curriculum without us noticin'. Should we stick to print just to have a permanent record?

The internet filters in the schools are blockin' legitimate Gaelic cultural sites because the English-based algorithms misinterpret certain words or themes as 'inappropriate'. We're fightin' a firewall that doesn't understand our culture.

BBC Alba is movin' more content to iPlayer, but the broadband in the glens is shockin'. By switchin' off the broadcast signal eventually, are they disenfranchisin' the very heartland audience that kept the language alive, just to chase the urban demographic?

Social media algorithms suppress content that isn't in English because they can't moderate it easily. Our Gaelic influencers are getting shadowbanned for speakin' their native tongue. Do we demand transparency or build our own platform?

A production company wants to use deepfake tech to dub mainstream Hollywood movies into Gaelic. It might get the kids watchin', but it looks uncanny and weird. Is it better to have bad lip-sync and great Gaelic, or AI-generated lips that look real but feel fake?

Data shows that 'twee' content—Highland cows and Outlander fantasies—gets more clicks than real documentaries about crofting struggles. If MG Alba chases the clicks, we lose our authentic voice. How do we balance viability with truth?

Auto-captioning on videos is terrible for Gaelic, often producing offensive gibberish. But manual captioning is expensive. Is it better to have no subtitles and exclude learners/deaf audiences, or have AI subtitles that butcher the language?

Tourists are usin' Instagram geotags to find 'secret' wild swimming spots and fragile machair, causin' erosion and mess. Should we be askin' platforms to hide the location data of our most vulnerable landscapes?

There's an archive of old Gaelic songs digitised online, but it's behind a paywall owned by a university. The songs belong to the people, but the server costs money. Is it right to sell our own culture back to us?

Targeted ads are pushin' holiday homes in the Hebrides to wealthy folks in London and New York. The algorithm is actively acceleration' depopulation by marketin' our homes as investments. Can we petition ad networks to stop targetin' our housing stock?

They're digitisin' the records of the Highland Clearances. An AI analysis suggests some local families who claim to be victims were actually complicit. This data could tear the community apart. Do we publish the raw truth or let the sleeping dogs lie for the sake of social cohesion?

Ancestry websites are selling 'Clan Heritage' packages to Americans based on shaky algorithms. It's commodifyin' our history and turnin' clan connection into a generic badge for purchase. How do we protect the dignity of the lineage against commercial database mining?

A developer wants to build an Augmented Reality app that overlays the burning cottages of the Clearances on the modern landscape. Is this powerful education, or is it trauma porn that turns our ancestors' suffering into a spectacle for tourists?

We have 3D scans of the Callanish Stones. A video game company wants to buy the data to put the stones in a fantasy game where they get blown up. They own the scan copyright. Do we have moral rights over the digital twin of a sacred site?

DNA testing is revealing non-paternity events in the clan lines from 200 years ago. It's challenging the chieftainships and land claims. Should genetic data override centuries of oral tradition and established custom?

AI restoration of old photos from the 1800s is smoothin' out the faces of the crofters, makin' them look healthy and clean when they were starvin'. It's rewriting the visual history of our hardship. Should we ban AI 'enhancement' of historical archives?

Digital mapping of common grazings is being proposed to settle disputes, but the old boundaries were defined by rocks and streams known only to the locals. Putting it on a precise GPS grid removes the flexibility and negotiation that kept the peace. Is precision always better?

A project wants to record the 'last speakers' of a specific dialect. It feels like vulture capitalism—waitin' for them to die to monetise the recordings. Shouldn't the focus be on creatin' *new* speakers instead of archivin' the death of the old?

The ferry booking system is entirely online now, driven by dynamic pricing algorithms. The locals can't book a slot to get to the hospital because the tourists book them all up months in advance. Is it ethical for public transport to prioritise profit over lifeline services?

Remote working tech has brought 'digital nomads' to the islands. They earn London wages and outbid the locals for housing, but they don't contribute to the crofting work or the community events. Is high-speed internet saving the island or killing its soul?

We're lookin' at a community land buyout, and they want to run the vote via a secure app. But the oldest crofters don't use smartphones. If we move democracy online, are we disenfranchising the people who know the land best?

Telehealth robots are being trialled to check on the elderly in the remote glens. It saves the nurse a two-hour drive, but that visit was the only human contact that person had all week. Is efficiency worth the isolation?

The new wind farm is offering 'community benefit' payments via cryptocurrency to bypass bureaucracy. It sounds modern, but it feels like a way to dodge proper oversight and tax. Should a crofting community be dealing in crypto?

Drones are being used to monitor sheep on the hill. It saves the legs, but the skill of the shepherd and the dog is being lost. If we automate the croft, do we lose the connection to the animal and the land?

A datacentre wants to open in the Highlands, promising jobs and using our renewable energy. But it uses massive amounts of water and power, while locals are in fuel poverty. Are we becoming a battery for the world's data while we freeze?

Online genealogy groups are great, but now strangers from abroad are arriving and walking onto working crofts demanding to see 'their' ancestral home, ignoring the privacy of the people living there now. Does digital data create a false sense of ownership?

The Masjid committee in Pollokshields is wantin' tae install facial recognition cameras at the doors. They say it's for security after that graffiti attack last month, aye? But my Uncle is pure raging, sayin' it's nae right for the government or police tae potentially get that data on who comes tae pray and when. Is it right tae trade our spiritual privacy for a bit of physical safety?

There's a new 'Halal Finder' app popular in Glasgow right now. It shows ye aw the takeaways and butchers, pure handy. But we found out it's sellin' location data tae third parties, trackin' exactly where the Muslim community moves aboot the city. Should we be boycotting a tool that helps the community just 'cause it's spyin' on us?

My cousin applyin' for loans tae start his business in Govanhill keeps gettin' knocked back by the bank's AI. We reckon it's postcode profiling, aye? Even though he's got the cash flow, the computer sees 'G42' and thinks 'high risk'. Is it ethical for banks tae use automatic systems that effectively redline oor neighbourhoods?

The NHS is trialling a genetic screening AI for the Pakistani community here to flag risks of cousins marryin'. It's meant tae help avoid health issues in the weans, I get that. But it feels like we're being singled out and stigmatised by a machine. Does public health trump the cultural sensitivity of how we choose our partners?

Grandad speaks mostly Punjabi and a bit of broad Glaswegian. We got him a smart speaker tae help him with lights and heating, but the thing doesnae understand a word he says. It only works if he puts on a 'posh' voice he doesnae have. Is it right tae sell tech in Scotland that cannae understand the folk actually livin' here?

A lot of the aunties use WhatsApp groups for community news in Glasgow. But now there's automated bots spreading fake news aboot vaccines and politics in Urdu, and the encryption means nobody can moderate it. Should the app break its privacy rules tae stop the misinformation spreadin' in our closed groups?

The school in the Southside is usin' AI to grade essays now. My wee sister writes with a mix of Scottish slang and sentence structures from home, and the AI keeps marking her down as 'ungrammatical'. It's forcing her tae write like a robot just tae pass. Is that nae just erasing her identity?

Police Scotland wants tae use predictive policing software. They say it'll allocate resources better, but we ken fine well it'll just send more patrols tae Pollokshields and Govanhill based on old arrest data. Is it ethical to use a system that turns historical bias into future harassment?

Since Brexit, we've nae got physical papers, just this digital status. My pal's phone died right at the border control coming back tae Edinburgh, and he couldnae prove he had the right tae be here. Is it ethical to force a digital-only existence on us where a dead battery means ye lose yer rights?

I'm working agency shifts in a warehouse, and they've got us wearing these smart wristbands tae track 'productivity'. It buzzes if ye stop pickin' for more than a minute. It feels like we're robots, not people. Is this level of surveillance justified just tae get parcels oot faster?

The council is cutting human translators and telling Polish folk tae just use Google Translate for housing forms. But the machine gets the legal terms wrong, and folk are ending up liable for things they didnae understand. Is it right to replace a skilled human with free AI when people's homes are at risk?

There's a landlord database startin' up that tracks tenants across Scotland. If ye complain aboot mould or repairs, ye get flagged as 'trouble'. For the Polish community, who often rent privately, this could leave us homeless. Should tech be used tae blacklist folk for demanding basic rights?

My workplace in Leith wants tae bring in fingerprint scanning for clocking in. They say it stops 'buddy punching', but a lot of us are worried aboot where that data goes, especially with the Home Office looking for reasons to deport folk. Do we have a right tae refuse biometric collection at work?

On the local community Facebook pages, the auto-mod AI keeps deleting posts written in Polish because it can't moderate them for 'hate speech'. We're trying to organise community support, but we're being silenced by a bot that only speaks English. Is that fair?

I changed my name on my CV from 'Wojciech' to 'William' and suddenly the automated hiring system started giving me interviews. The AI is clearly trained to prefer Anglo names. Is it ethical for recruitment platforms tae operate without auditing for this kind of bias?

Sending money home to family is getting harder with these new banking apps asking for endless verification. The facial rec struggles with lighting in my flat, and if it fails, they freeze my account. Why should access tae my own wages depend on whether an algorithm likes my selfie?

The Home Office puts us in hotels and gives us these Aspen cards for food. We ken they track every penny—where we shop, what we buy. It feels like we're criminals just for seeking safety. Is it ethical tae trade basic sustenance for total loss of privacy?

They're using an algorithm tae decide where to disperse refugees across Scotland. It sent my friend tae a tiny village in the Highlands where nobody looks like him and there's no halal food, just because the computer said there was 'capacity'. Should a machine decide where a human being rebuilds their life?

We use free messaging apps tae talk to family back in the conflict zone. But if the data isn't secure, the regime back home could find them. Is it right for tech companies to market 'privacy' when they still collect metadata that could get people killed?

Everything for asylum support is online now—legal aid, health appointments. But many of us arrive with no phone and no money for data. The system is designed for people who are already connected. Is digital-by-default ethical when it excludes the most vulnerable?

To get our weekly support money, we have to report to a centre and scan our fingerprints. It makes the weans feel like they're in a prison. Is this level of biometric control necessary for humanitarian aid?

The doctor used a translation app to tell me my diagnosis because no interpreter was available. The app got it wrong, and I was terrified for days thinking I was dying. Is it ethical to rely on imperfect AI for life-changing medical conversations?

For the community sponsorship scheme, the government uses automated background checks on host families. It flagged a kind Scottish family as 'unsuitable' because of a minor debt years ago. Should an algorithm prevent human connection and shelter?

I lost my papers fleeing the war. Now the UK tech systems can't verify who I am, so I don't exist in the database. I can't rent, can't work. Is it ethical for a society to make existence dependent on a digital record?

The council is flying drones over the site to count the trailers and check for 'unauthorised development'. They say it's for planning, but it feels like spying on our homes. Do we nae have a right to privacy just because we live in chalets and trailers?

The education authority wants the weans to use tablets that track their location to ensure they're 'attending' school when we're travelling. It feels like tagging them. Is it right to monitor Traveller children more strictly than settled ones?

Every time a local paper posts a story about a new stopping place online, the comments are pure vile, full of hate against Travellers. The platforms do nothing to stop it. Is it ethical for tech giants to profit from engagement driven by racism against our community?

You need a fixed postcode for everything online—GP registration, insurance, ordering parts. The systems literally won't let you type in a site address sometimes. Is it ethical to design digital infrastructure that erases our way of life?

Researchers came and recorded our songs and stories for a digital archive. Now they put it behind a paywall online, and we have to pay to hear our own grandfather's voice. Is that nae stealing our culture?

Some of the recycling centres are using facial recognition and number plate reading to ban vans they think are commercial. It's barring Travellers just for taking rubbish to the tip in our own vehicles. Is this tech being weaponised to stop us using public services?

The new NHS app reminds you of appointments, but it assumes you can get there in 20 minutes. When we're shifted on by police and have to move miles away, we miss the slot and get struck off. Should health tech account for nomadic lifestyles?

We hear the police use data mapping to predict where unauthorised camps might start. They're waiting for us before we even pull up. Is it ethical to use data to preemptively block our freedom of movement?

There's a new app for reporting hate crimes in Scotland. It asks for video evidence and precise GPS data. If ye don't have that, it doesn't log the report. Does this tech suppress the true scale of racism by setting the bar too high for victims?

Police Scotland is trialling live facial recognition. We ken from studies it misidentifies brown and black faces more often. If they switch that on in Glasgow city centre, are they knowingly putting minorities at risk of wrongful arrest?

An AI tool used in Scottish hospitals to prioritise emergency care relies on historical data. If that data shows minorities historically received less pain management, the AI might deprioritise us now. Is it ethical to deploy 'objective' tools built on subjective racism?

Social housing allocation is automated now. It prioritises 'local connection', which disadvantages refugees and new migrants who haven't been in the borough for 5 years. Is this just a digital way of keeping neighbourhoods segregated?

A big Glasgow firm uses AI to scan video interviews for 'cultural fit'. It marks down accents that aren't 'Standard English'. This hits Scots speakers, but it hits migrants even harder. Is 'cultural fit' just code for 'sounds white'?
